(Makkan, except verses 12, 17 and 114, which are Madinan; it has 123 verses; it was revealed after Surah Yunus.) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm (uhkimat), then made distinct (fussilat), from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾ The verb uhkimat means: its verses were arranged in a firm, solid composition, free of any contradiction or defect, like a well-built, tightly fitted edifice.

It is also permissible that it be a causative form with the hamza, from hakama (with a damma on the kaf), meaning "to become wise" (hakim): i.e., its verses were made wise, as in His words, ﴿the verses of the Wise Book﴾. It was also said: they were prevented from corruption, from the expression ahkamtu al-dabba, "I placed a bridle (hikma) on the beast to restrain it from bolting." Jarir said:

"O Banu Hanifa, bridle your foolish ones (uhkimu sufahaakum),
Indeed I fear that I will become angry at you (an aghdaba)."

(Jarir means: O Banu Hanifa, "restrain your foolish ones from me, just as a beast is restrained by a bridle, for my anger toward you is severe." There is in it a kind of threat; his fear for them is a metaphor for that. The clause "an aghdaba" is the object of "akhaafu," i.e., I fear for you my anger.)

From Qatada: "they were made firm against falsehood, then distinguished, just as necklaces are arranged with pearls, [containing] the proofs of Tawhid, the rulings, the admonitions, and the stories. Or they were made into sections, surah by surah and verse by verse, and were revealed in parts and not all at once. Or what the servants need was explained within it: i.e., it was clarified and summarized." It is also read: "uhkimat ayatuhu thumma fussilat," meaning: I made them firm, then I distinguished them.

From Ikrima and al-Dahhak: "thumma fussilat," i.e., it distinguished between truth and falsehood.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "thumma" (then)? I say: it does not mean temporal succession, but succession in rank, as when you say: "it is most excellently firm, then most excellently distinct," and "so-and-so is noble in origin, then noble in deed."

"Kitab" is the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mubtada' mahdhuf). "Uhkimat" is its attribute. His words, ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾, are a second attribute. It is permissible that it be a predicate after a predicate, or that it be a complement (silah) of "uhkimat" and "fussilat," meaning: from Him is its firmness and its distinction. There is in it a fine antithesis (tibaq), because the meaning is: its firmness is by the Wise, and its distinction, i.e., its explanation and elaboration, is by the One Aware, who knows the modes of affairs.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 2–4:

Allā taʿbudū (أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا) is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), in the sense of: "lest you worship." Or the "an" (أَن) may be explanatory (mufassira), because in the detailing of the verses there is the meaning of speech, as if it were said: "He said: do not worship except Allah," or "He commanded you that you not worship except Allah." Wa-an istaghfirū (وَأَنِ اسْتَغْفِرُوا), that is, He commanded you to monotheism and seeking forgiveness.

It is permissible that this be an independent statement, cut off from what precedes it, on the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ), as an incitement from him to the exclusivity of God in worship. This is indicated by His saying: "Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good news" (إِنَّنِي لَكُمْ مِنْهُ نَذِيرٌ وَبَشِيرٌ). It is as if he said: "Leave off worshipping other than God; indeed I am to you from Him a warner," like His saying, "So strike the necks" (فَضَرْبَ الرِّقابِ). The pronoun in "from Him" (مِنْهُ) refers to God, Mighty and Majestic, meaning: "Indeed I am to you a warner and a bringer of good news from Him," like His saying, "a messenger from Allah" (رَسُولٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ). Or it is connected to "warner" (نَذِيرٌ), meaning: "I warn you of Him and of His punishment if you disbelieve, and I give you good news of His reward if you believe."

If you ask: what is the meaning of "then" (ثُمَّ) in His saying, "Then repent to Him" (ثُمَّ تُوبُوا إِلَيْهِ)? I say: its meaning is: seek forgiveness from polytheism, then return to Him through obedience. Or: seek forgiveness, and seeking forgiveness is repentance, then make repentance sincere and remain steadfast in it, like His saying, "Then remain steadfast" (ثُمَّ اسْتَقامُوا).

"He will give you enjoyment" (يُمَتِّعْكُمْ): He will prolong your benefit in this world with good, pleasing benefits, from a wide livelihood and continuous blessing, "until a specified term" (إِلى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى), that is, until He takes your souls, like His saying, "We will surely cause him to live a good life" (فَلَنُحْيِيَنَّهُ حَياةً طَيِّبَةً). "And He will give every possessor of virtue his virtue" (وَيُؤْتِ كُلَّ ذِي فَضْلٍ فَضْلَهُ): He will give in the Hereafter every one who had virtue in action, and an increase in it, as recompense for his virtue, without diminishing anything of it.

Or "his virtue" means his virtue in reward, and ranks in Paradise vary according to the variation of acts of obedience.

"But if they turn away" (وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا): if they turn away, "I fear for you the punishment of a great day" (عَذابَ يَوْمٍ كَبِيرٍ), which is the Day of Resurrection, described as great just as it is described as mighty and heavy. The great day's punishment is clarified by the fact that their return is to One who is capable of all things, so He is able to inflict the most severe of what He wills of their punishment, and nothing can frustrate Him.

It is recited: "wa-in tawallā" (وإن تولوا), from "walā" (ولى).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 5:**

﴿يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ﴾: they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever turns toward something faces it with his chest, and whoever turns away from it and deviates, bends his chest away from it and folds his side away from it. ﴿لِيَسْتَخْفُوا مِنْهُ﴾ means: they intend to hide from God, so that His Messenger and the believers do not notice their turning away. A parallel to the implied "they intend" (idmar, ellipsis of a word understood from context), since the meaning requires it [[His words "since the meaning requires it" mean: for the meaning to be conveyed. (ʿAli)]], is the implied element in God's words ﴿اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ الْبَحْرَ فَانْفَلَقَ﴾ (Q 26:63: "Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted"), whose meaning is: "So he struck, and it parted."

The meaning of ﴿أَلا حِينَ يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيابَهُمْ﴾ (Q 11:5: "Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments") is: they intend to hide even when they cover themselves with their garments, out of aversion to hearing the speech of God, like the words of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿جَعَلُوا أَصابِعَهُمْ فِي آذانِهِمْ وَاسْتَغْشَوْا ثِيابَهُمْ﴾ (Q 71:7: "They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments"). Then He said: ﴿يَعْلَمُ ما يُسِرُّونَ وَما يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ (Q 11:5: "He knows what they conceal and what they reveal"), meaning: there is no difference in His knowledge between their secret and their open speech, so there is no way for them to reach what they desire of concealment. God observes their folding of their chests and their covering themselves with garments, and their hypocrisy is not hidden from Him.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who used to show love to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), had a sweet tongue and a fine manner of speech, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would be pleased by his company and conversation, while he was concealing the opposite of what he showed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

It is read as *tathnūnī ṣudūruhum* (with the final ه-substitute changed), and *ithnawnī* (the pattern *if'awʿala*, from *al-thanī*, "bending"), like *iḥlawlā* from *al-ḥalāwa* ("sweetness"), which is a pattern of intensification (*binā' mubālagha*), read with the letter *tāʾ* or *yāʾ*. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: *la-tathnūnī*. It is also read *tathnūnn*, its original form being *tathnawnin* (pattern *tafʿawʿala*), from *al-thunn* [[In al-Sihah, *al-thunn* with a kasra means the drying of grass (ʿAli).]], which is what is soft and weak of herbage, meaning: their chests yield to bending, as soft plants bend. Or it means the weakness of their faith and the sickness of their hearts. It is also read *tathnaʾin*, from *iṭnaʾanna* (pattern *if'alla*) of it, then the hamza was introduced, as it is said: *ibyaḍḍat* and *adhhāmmat* [[Here Zamakhshari cites forms with hamza substituted for a doubled or glided letter, as in *ibyaḍḍa* and *iddhāmma*-type formations (ʿAli).]]. It is also read *tathnawā*, on the pattern of *tarʿawī*.

[[Zamakhshari said: "If you say, 'How did He say, ﴿upon Allah is their provision﴾ with the wording of obligation...' etc." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: Whatever provision Allah grants to a beast or a responsible person in this world, or reward in the Hereafter, is all bounty (fadl), and nothing is obligatory upon Allah the Exalted. If such a form of expression occurs, it is to be understood as follows: when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, promised them His bounty, and His promise is information and His information is true, the occurrence of what was promised became necessary, meaning it is impossible by reason that it should not occur, because the contradiction of the report of the truthful would follow. So this was expressed with what is used to express the obligation of duty, and between the two there is the difference mentioned. This is the principle of the People of Truth (ahl al-haqq). The discussion of it has already passed at His words, ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah﴾, and Allah is the Granter of success.]] Is it not merely bounty? I say: It is bounty, but since He guaranteed to bestow it upon them, the bounty became obligatory, like the vows of servants. And "al-mustaqarr" (the place of settlement): its place on the earth and its dwelling. And "al-mustawda'" (the place of deposit): where it was deposited before settling, from a loin, or a womb, or an egg. Every one of the beasts, its provision, its settlement and its deposit are in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh); that is, its mention is written in it, clear.

And His Throne was upon the water: that is, there was nothing beneath it of creation before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and its elevation was above them, [with] nothing but the water. This is evidence that the Throne and the water were created before the heavens and the earth.

It was said: "And the water was [[The phrase 'It was said: and the water was', perhaps it should be 'was' without the conjunction 'wa'. It is possible that the meaning is: His Throne was upon the water, and the water was. (ʿAyn)]] upon the back of the wind." God knows best about that. Whatever the case, God holds all of that in His power, and the more massive the bodies are, the more they need Him and His holding them. ﴿That He may test you﴾ is connected to "created": that is, He created them for a profound wisdom, which is that He makes them dwellings for His servants, bestows upon them blessings of every kind within them, and imposes upon them obedience and abstention from disobedience. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He rewards; whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes. Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said: "that He may test you." He means: that He may do to you what one who tests does, in order to see how you act. If you say: how is the verb of testing made dependent [on a clause with an interrogative]? I say: because testing contains the meaning of knowledge, since it is a path to it, so it is associated with it, just as you say: "Look which of them is better in appearance, and listen which of them is better in voice," because looking and listening are paths to knowledge. If you say: how was it said ﴿which of you is best in deed﴾, when the deeds of believers are those that vary between good and better, whereas the deeds of believers and disbelievers vary between good and bad? I say: those who are best in deed are the God-fearing, who have hastened to attain what is God's aim from His servants. So He singled them out for mention and dropped mention of those behind them, to honour them and to draw attention to their station with Him, and so that this would be a kindness to the listeners and an encouragement to attain their excellence. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "That He may test you, which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of God, and quickest in obedience to God." [[Dawud ibn al-Mujabbar recorded it in the Book of the Intellect, and al-Harith in his Musnad from him, and al-Tabari and Ibn Mardawayh from his route, from ʿAbd al-Wahid ibn Zayd, from Kulayb ibn Wa'il, from Ibn ʿUmar. Dawud is discarded. Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from the route of Muhammad ibn Amras, from Sulayman ibn ʿIsa, from al-Thawri, from Kulayb in the same way, and its chain is weaker than the first.]]

It was recited: ﴿And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected,"﴾ with the hamza vowelled with a fatḥa (إنكم mistaken as "أنكم").

Its explanation: it may be from their saying: "Go to the market for us, so that (عنك) you buy meat for us," and "annaka" (أنك) is used in the sense of "ʿallaka" (لعلك), meaning: "If you say to them, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,' [treating it as] an expectation of their resurrection and an assumption, and do not decisively state the matter by denying it, they would say: ﴿This is nothing but evident magic,﴾ decisively stating its falsehood." It is also permissible that "qulta" (قلت) be taken to include the meaning of "dhakartu" (ذكرت, "you mentioned"). The meaning of their saying ﴿This is nothing but evident magic﴾ is that magic is a false matter, and its falsehood is like the falsehood of magic, a comparison to it. Or they pointed by "this" to the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is what speaks of the resurrection; so when they made it magic, they included within that the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other things. It was also recited: ﴿This is nothing but a sorcerer,﴾ meaning the Messenger, and the sorcerer is a liar and a falsifier.

The punishment: the punishment of the Hereafter. It is also said: the punishment of the Day of Badr. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: Gabriel killed the mockers. "Up to a community" means up to a group, up to a set period of time. "What holds it back" means what prevents it from descending, [said] in haste as a form of denial and mockery. "On the day it comes to them" is in the accusative, governed by the predicate of laysa (not). Those who permit placing the predicate of laysa before laysa use this as evidence, because if the complement of its predicate may be placed before it, this is evidence that its predicate may also be placed before it, since the complement follows the governing word, so it occurs only where the governing word occurs. "And there befell them" means it surrounded them. "That which they used to mock" means the punishment they used to hasten. He put "they mock" in place of "they hasten" because their hastening was by way of mockery. The meaning is: it will befall them, but it came in the manner of God's habit in His reports.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 9–11:

﴿Al-insan﴾ (the human being) is generic (li-l-jins). ﴿Rahmah﴾ (mercy) means a blessing: health, security, and wealth. ﴿Thumma naza'nahā minhu﴾ (then We took it away from him): then We stripped that blessing from him. ﴿Innahu la-ya'us﴾ (indeed he is despairing): he is extremely hopeless that such a blessing will return to him after it has been taken away. He has cut off his hope in the vastness of Allah's bounty, without patience, without submission to His decree, and without seeking restoration (istirja'). ﴿Kafur﴾ (ungrateful): greatly ungrateful for the past blessings of Allah in which he had been fluctuating. ﴿Nassa'un﴾ (forgetful/ungrateful for what he had): ﴿Dhahaba al-sayyi'at 'anni﴾ (the misfortunes have gone from me), i.e., the calamities that afflicted me. ﴿Innahu la-farihun﴾ (indeed he is exultant): insolent and boastful. ﴿Fakhur﴾ (boastful) toward people because of the blessings Allah has made him taste. Joy and boasting have preoccupied him from giving thanks.

﴿Illa alladhina amanu﴾ (except those who believed): for their custom, if mercy reaches them, is to give thanks, and if a blessing is removed from them, is to be patient.

﴿Illa alladhina amanu﴾ (except those who believed): for their custom, if mercy reaches them, is to give thanks, and if a blessing is removed from them, is to be patient.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 12:

They used to propose to him signs out of obstinacy, not out of a desire for guidance, for if they had been seeking guidance, one sign from what he brought would have been sufficient for their guidance. Among their proposals were ﴿Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?﴾ They did not give any weight to the Qur'an, and they treated it and other clear proofs that he brought with contempt. So the breast of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would constrict at having to convey to them what they would not accept and would mock. Therefore Allah stirred him up and roused him to perform the message and to disregard their rejection, their mockery and their proposals, by His saying: ﴿So perhaps you may leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾, meaning: perhaps you may refrain from delivering it to them and conveying it to them, out of fear of their rejection of it and their contempt for it, ﴿and your breast may be constricted by it﴾, by reciting it to them, ﴿lest they say﴾, out of fear that they would say, ﴿"Why has a treasure not been sent down to him?"﴾, meaning: why was there not sent down to him what we proposed, of treasure and angels, and why was there not sent down to him what we do not desire or propose? Then He said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: it is incumbent upon you only to warn them with what has been revealed to you and to convey what you were commanded to convey, and it is not your concern whether they reject it, disregard it or propose things. ﴿And Allah is Guardian over all things﴾, meaning: He watches over what they say, and He will do with them what must be done. So rely upon Him, entrust your affair to Him, and convey the revelation with an open heart and an expanded breast, not turning to their arrogance nor caring for their foolishness and mockery.

If you ask: why did he switch from ḍayyiq (ضيق) to ḍā'iq (ضائق)? I answer: to show that it is a passing, non-permanent constriction, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the most expansive-hearted of people. A similar usage is your saying: "Zayd is a sayyid (سيد) and a jawād (جواد)," meaning the lasting and established lordship and generosity; but if you want to indicate occurrence, you say: sā'id (سائد) and jā'id (جائد), and the like. [Reading: "they were a people ʿāmmūn" (عامين) in some recitations.] And the verse of al-Samhari al-ʿUkli:

*In a barren land, where the miser grows fat there, while the noble of people are seen with their faces wan.*

[Note on the verse: al-ʿUkli. Al-shuḥūb means change of colour. Abu Zayd recited it as evidence that al-shuḥūb in the dialect of Banu Kilab means emaciation, which fits the antithesis better with his saying "a barren land." The miser, whose concern is his belly, is "fat" (sāmin) there because of his much eating. As for the noble people, they are changed and emaciated there, because they feed others and do not eat themselves. The form fāʿil from samina is irregular (shādh); its regular form would be fa‘īl.]

Or do they say, "He has invented it"? The pronoun in "iftarahu" refers to what has been revealed to you. He first challenged them with ten surahs, then with a single surah, just as a teacher of calligraphy says to his student: "Write ten lines similar to what I write." When the student's inability to match his handwriting becomes clear, the teacher says: "I have settled for you with one line like it," meaning "like its equivalents," going by the fact that each of them is similar to it. "Muftarayat" (fabricated) is an attribute of "ten surahs." When they said, "You have invented the Qur'an and fabricated it on your own, and it is not from God," he (God) went along with their claim (qawadahum, here meaning he agreed with them and accommodated them) and gave them free rein, saying: "Suppose I have fabricated it from myself and it was not revealed to me, and the matter is as you say, then you too produce speech like it, fabricated from yourselves. For you are eloquent Arabs, like me, and you will not be unable to match what I am able to produce of speech." If you ask: How can what they produce be "like it," when what they produce is fabricated and this (the Qur'an) is not fabricated? I answer: its likeness lies in the excellence of its eloquence and composition, even though it is fabricated.

**Question:** If you ask: what is the reason for shifting to the plural address in His words ﴿لَكُمْ فَاعْلَمُوا﴾ (*lakum fa-'lamu*, "for you, then know") after the singular in His words ﴿قُلْ﴾ (*qul*, "say")?

**Answer:** I say: its meaning is, "If they do not respond to you and to the believers," because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers were challenging them. In another place He says: ﴿فَإِنْ لَمْ يَسْتَجِيبُوا لَكَ فَاعْلَمْ﴾ ("If they do not respond to you, then know").

It is also permissible that the plural is used to honour the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as in the verse of the poet:

*fa-in shi'tu harramtu al-nisa'a siwakum*
("If I wish, I will forbid women other than you").

[[The explanation of this evidence has been given in the first volume, p. 294, so consult it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

**Another interpretation:** The address is to the polytheists, and the pronoun in ﴿فَإِلَّمْ يَسْتَجِيبُوا﴾ ("if they do not respond") refers to ﴿مَنِ اسْتَطَعْتُمْ﴾ ("whomever you can"). The meaning is: if those whom you call upon besides God do not respond to you by helping you to oppose it (the Qur'an), since they know their inability to do so and that their strength is too weak to reach it, then ﴿فَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّمَا أُنْزِلَ بِعِلْمِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("know that it was revealed with the knowledge of God"), that is, it was revealed containing what none knows but God: a composition inimitable by creation, and reports of unseen matters to which they have no access. ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا﴾ ("and know") at that point ﴿أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ﴾ ("that there is no deity except God") alone, and that His unity is obligatory, and that associating others with Him is a great wrong. ﴿فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("will you then submit?"), that is, will you pledge yourselves to Islam after this decisive proof? This is a good and consistent interpretation.

As for the one who makes the address to the Muslims, its meaning is: "Remain steadfast upon the knowledge you have, and increase in certainty and firmness of foot, that it was sent down from God and in (affirming) the unity of God."

**The meaning of ﴿فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾:** "So are you sincere?" (i.e., "are you sincere?")

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 15–16:

We shall pay them in full (nuwaffi ilayhim) their deeds' rewards, complete and without diminution, in this world, which is what they are given there of health and provision. And it has been said: they are the people of showing off (riya'). It is said to the reciters among them: "You wanted it said: so-and-so is a reciter," and so it was said. And to the one who keeps up the ties of kinship and gives charity: "You did it so that it would be said," and so it was said. And to the one who fights and is killed: "You fought so that it would be said, 'So-and-so is brave,'" and so it was said. It is also related from Anas ibn Malik: they are the Jews and Christians, who, if they give to a beggar or keep up the ties of kinship, have the reward of that hastened to them in the form of expansion in provision and health of body. And it has been said: they are those hypocrites who fought alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so they were given a share of the spoils.

It is also read yuwaff (with the ya'), on the basis that the verb is attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And tuwaff ilayhim a'maluhum (with the ta'), in the passive form. In the reading of al-Hasan: nawfi, with the lightening (takhfif) and the retention of the ya', because the condition occurred in the past tense, as in his saying:

"He says, 'Neither my wealth nor my family is absent'"

[[The explanation of this witness has been given in the first part, page 537; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

*And what they did in it came to nothing (wa habita ma sana'u fiha)*: and in the Hereafter what they did came to nothing, or their handiwork. The meaning is: there was no reward for them, because they did not intend by it the Hereafter; they intended only this world, and what they intended was paid to them in full. *And vain is what they used to do (wa batilun ma kanu ya'maluna)*, that is, their deed in itself was vain, because it was not done for a correct purpose, and a vain deed has no reward.

It is also read wa butila (with the verb in the passive). And it is related from 'Asim: wa batilan with the accusative, and in this there are two possibilities: that ma be indefinite (ibhamiyya), governing ya'maluna, meaning: "and vain, whatever vanity they were doing"; or that it be in the sense of the verbal noun, so that the meaning is: "and their deeds came to vanity in the manner of vanity" (wa butila butlanan ma kanu ya'maluna).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 17:

﴿Is he who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ means: "Is he who is [like] one who desires the life of this world, [or] he who is upon clear evidence?" [[The phrase "fa-man kana ʿala bayyina" is in the words of al-Nasafi: "like one who desires..." etc. (ʿA.)]] That is, they are not equal to them in rank, nor do they come close to them. He intends that there is a vast disparity and a clear distinction between the two groups. By "them" he means those among the Jews who believed, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and others. "Upon clear evidence from his Lord" means upon proof from God and a demonstration that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the evidence of reason. ﴿And there follows it﴾ means: and this proof is followed by ﴿a witness from Him﴾, that is, a witness testifying to its truth, and this is the Qur'an, ﴿from Him﴾, from God, or a witness from the Qur'an, since it was mentioned just before. ﴿And before it﴾, that is, before the Qur'an, ﴿was the Book of Moses﴾, which is the Torah. That is: this proof is also followed by the Book of Moses before the Qur'an.

It is also read as "Kitaba Musa" with the accusative, and its meaning is: he who was upon clear evidence from his Lord, which is the proof that the Qur'an is true, and ﴿there follows it﴾: the Qur'an is recited, ﴿a witness from Him﴾, a witness from among those who were upon clear evidence, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Q. 46:10], and His saying: ﴿Say: "God suffices as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [Q. 13:43]. ﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾, that is, the Torah is recited before the Qur'an, ﴿as a guide﴾, an exemplar to be followed in religion, a model in it, ﴿and a mercy﴾, a great blessing upon those to whom it was sent. ﴿Those﴾, that is, those who were upon clear evidence, ﴿believe in it﴾, they believe in the Qur'an. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it among the factions﴾, that is, the people of Mecca and those who supported them from among the factions that banded together against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿the Fire is their promised place﴾. ﴿So be not in doubt about it﴾. It is also read as "mirya" with a dammah, and both mean doubt, ﴿about it﴾, that is, about the Qur'an or about the promised place.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 11, verses 18–22:**

﴿They will be presented before their Lord﴾: they will be held in the place of standing (al-mawqif), and their deeds will be displayed. ﴿And the witnesses will testify against them﴾: the witnesses (al-ashhad) are from among the angels and the prophets, that ﴿these are the ones who lied against Allah﴾, claiming that He has taken a son and a partner. It will be said: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, so woe to their disgrace and woe to their exposure!

Al-ashhad is the plural of shahid or shahid, like ashab or ashraf.

﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾: they describe it as crooked while it is straight. Or, they seek to make its people crooked by apostasy. ﴿They are the ones who disbelieve in the Hereafter﴾ is repeated to emphasize their disbelief in it and their being singled out for it.

﴿Those were not able to escape [Allah] in the earth﴾: that is, they could not have eluded Allah in the world from punishing them, had He wished to punish them. ﴿And they had no protectors who could help them against Him﴾ or shield them from His punishment. But He willed to give them respite and to delay their punishment until this Day. This is part of the speech of the witnesses.

﴿The punishment will be doubled for them﴾. It is also recited as yudda'af (with the meaning of doubling).

﴿They could not hear﴾: he means that, because of their extreme deafness to hearing the truth and their aversion to it, it is as though they were unable to hear.

[Mahmud said: "He means that, because of their extreme deafness to hearing the truth and their aversion to it, it is as though they..." etc.] Ahmad said: The people of truth, although they deny that the human capacity (istita'a) has any effect and attribute all creation to the power of the Creator, Exalted is He, do not deny the human capacity itself, nor what a person finds within himself of the difference between forced movements and voluntary ones. What denies capacity entirely are in reality the Jabriyya (determinists), not the people of the Sunna. The truth is with al-Zamakhshari in this place, except in his heedlessness when he says: "he howls at the people of justice (ahl al-'adl) with it," meaning the aforementioned verse. This is a great slip. Even granting that the determinist erred in using the verse as evidence for his doctrine, how can he permit himself to call the citing of the verse a howling? He was reciting the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, though his error lay in using it to confirm his false doctrine. Al-Zamakhshari is extremely lax regarding the etiquette that is required toward the Noble Book. Such leniency is fitting only when one is explaining the poetry of Imru' al-Qays or al-Harith ibn Hilliza. As for the etiquette of the Qur'an, it cannot tolerate even something easier than that. And Allah is the Granter of success.

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "And perhaps some of the determinists..."] If by "the determinists" he means the people of the Sunna, as is his habit, then they do not deny the servant capacity in the act. Rather, they affirm for him acquisition (kasb) and capacity together with the act. If he means those who hold pure determinism, that the servant is like a feather suspended in the air, then there is no harm in it. Al-Khazin reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse that he said: Allah, Exalted is He, informed that He prevented the people of polytheism from obeying Him in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, He said: ﴿they could not hear﴾, which is obedience to Him, ﴿and they could not see﴾. As for the Hereafter, He said: ﴿they will not be able [to hear]; their eyes will be humbled﴾. (Gh.)

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "he howls with it"] In al-Sihah: al-wa'wa'a is the cry of the wolf. (Gh.)

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "they will not be able..."] "Those who lost their souls": they bought the worship of idols in exchange for the worship of Allah, so their loss in this trade is the greatest loss there could be, namely that they lost their own souls. ﴿And what they used to invent went astray from them﴾: it was lost and perished from them, what they had bought, namely the idols and their intercession. ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. He explains this elsewhere: ﴿They are the greatest losers﴾. You will not see anyone more clearly losing than them.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 11, verses 18–22:**

﴿They will be presented before their Lord﴾: they will be held in the place of standing (al-mawqif), and their deeds will be displayed. ﴿And the witnesses will testify against them﴾: the witnesses (al-ashhad) are from among the angels and the prophets, that ﴿these are the ones who lied against Allah﴾, claiming that He has taken a son and a partner. It will be said: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, so woe to their disgrace and woe to their exposure!

Al-ashhad is the plural of shahid or shahid, like ashab or ashraf.

﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾: they describe it as crooked while it is straight. Or, they seek to make its people crooked by apostasy. ﴿They are the ones who disbelieve in the Hereafter﴾ is repeated to emphasize their disbelief in it and their being singled out for it.

﴿Those were not able to escape [Allah] in the earth﴾: that is, they could not have eluded Allah in the world from punishing them, had He wished to punish them. ﴿And they had no protectors who could help them against Him﴾ or shield them from His punishment. But He willed to give them respite and to delay their punishment until this Day. This is part of the speech of the witnesses.

﴿The punishment will be doubled for them﴾. It is also recited as yudda'af (with the meaning of doubling).

﴿They could not hear﴾: he means that, because of their extreme deafness to hearing the truth and their aversion to it, it is as though they were unable to hear.

[Mahmud said: "He means that, because of their extreme deafness to hearing the truth and their aversion to it, it is as though they..." etc.] Ahmad said: The people of truth, although they deny that the human capacity (istita'a) has any effect and attribute all creation to the power of the Creator, Exalted is He, do not deny the human capacity itself, nor what a person finds within himself of the difference between forced movements and voluntary ones. What denies capacity entirely are in reality the Jabriyya (determinists), not the people of the Sunna. The truth is with al-Zamakhshari in this place, except in his heedlessness when he says: "he howls at the people of justice (ahl al-'adl) with it," meaning the aforementioned verse. This is a great slip. Even granting that the determinist erred in using the verse as evidence for his doctrine, how can he permit himself to call the citing of the verse a howling? He was reciting the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, though his error lay in using it to confirm his false doctrine. Al-Zamakhshari is extremely lax regarding the etiquette that is required toward the Noble Book. Such leniency is fitting only when one is explaining the poetry of Imru' al-Qays or al-Harith ibn Hilliza. As for the etiquette of the Qur'an, it cannot tolerate even something easier than that. And Allah is the Granter of success.

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "And perhaps some of the determinists..."] If by "the determinists" he means the people of the Sunna, as is his habit, then they do not deny the servant capacity in the act. Rather, they affirm for him acquisition (kasb) and capacity together with the act. If he means those who hold pure determinism, that the servant is like a feather suspended in the air, then there is no harm in it. Al-Khazin reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse that he said: Allah, Exalted is He, informed that He prevented the people of polytheism from obeying Him in this world and the Hereafter. As for this world, He said: ﴿they could not hear﴾, which is obedience to Him, ﴿and they could not see﴾. As for the Hereafter, He said: ﴿they will not be able [to hear]; their eyes will be humbled﴾. (Gh.)

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "he howls with it"] In al-Sihah: al-wa'wa'a is the cry of the wolf. (Gh.)

[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "they will not be able..."] "Those who lost their souls": they bought the worship of idols in exchange for the worship of Allah, so their loss in this trade is the greatest loss there could be, namely that they lost their own souls. ﴿And what they used to invent went astray from them﴾: it was lost and perished from them, what they had bought, namely the idols and their intercession. ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. He explains this elsewhere: ﴿They are the greatest losers﴾. You will not see anyone more clearly losing than them.

And they humbled themselves before their Lord, submitting to Him and devoting themselves to His worship with humility and lowliness. It is derived from al-khabt, which is low-lying land that is level and settled. From it comes their description of a thing as al-dani' al-khabit (the base, lowly thing). The poet said:

"The good, even if little, of provision benefits, while the abundant base (khabit) does not benefit"

[The explanation of this line of verse is given in the first part, p. 543; refer to it if you wish. Corrector's note.]

It has also been said that the taa' in it is a substitute for the thaa'.

He likened the group of the disbelievers to the blind and the deaf, and the group of the believers to the seeing and the hearing. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "He likened the group of the disbelievers to the blind and the deaf, and the group of the believers to the seeing and the hearing," up to his saying "that the waw be ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Unlike it according to the first aspect, for it is for conjoining the described to the described. As for his comparing the verse to the simile of Imru' al-Qays in that he likened [something] with two similes, there is room for consideration. For Imru' al-Qays likened each of the fresh and the dry [things] with one simile, whereas the verse, according to the first explanation, likened each of the disbeliever and the believer with two similes. The line of Imru' al-Qays is to be compared only according to the second aspect, for its implication is that each of the two was likened with one simile, but in two multiple attributes. The matter in this is minor, and God knows best.] This is from enfolding (al-laff) and antithesis (al-tibaq). It has two meanings: that the group be likened with two similes, as Imru' al-Qays likened the hearts of the birds to the withered date and the jujube; or that it be likened to the one who combined blindness and deafness, or the one who combined sight and hearing [Editor's note: his saying "or the one who combined sight and hearing," perhaps it is: "and the one who..." (ʿ)]. On the basis that the waw in ﴿وَالْأَصَمِّ﴾ and in ﴿وَالسَّمِيعِ﴾ is for conjoining the attribute to the attribute, as in his saying:

al-Ṣābiḥ fa-l-Ghānim fa-l-Āyib

﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِيَانِ مَثَلًا﴾: are the two equal in likeness? That is, the two groups, as a comparison.

[Editor's note: the explanation of this line has passed in the first part, p. 41, so refer to it if you wish. (his corrector)]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 25–26:

That is, We sent Noah "that I am a plain warner to you" (anni lakum nadhir). Its meaning is that We sent him accompanied by this statement, namely His saying ﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you﴾ with the kasra (in inni). Then, when the preposition was attached to it, it took the fatha, as the fatha occurs in "ka-anna" (as if), while the meaning remains that of the kasra, as in your saying: "Inna Zaydan ka-l-asad" (Indeed Zayd is like a lion). It has also been read with the kasra on the basis of intending speech (al-qawl). ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾ (an la ta'budu) is a substitution for ﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you﴾, meaning: We sent him that you worship none but Allah. Or "an" is explanatory (mufassira), connected to "We sent" or to "warner".

The attribution of "painful" (alim) to "the day" is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), since pain occurs in it. If you ask: what about when it is attributed to the punishment ('adhab)? I say: it is metaphorical likewise, because the one who truly experiences pain is the one being punished. A parallel to both is your saying: "Your day is fasting" (nahāruka sa'im), and "his grandfather's grandfather prospered" (jadda jaddahu).

I say: it is metaphorical likewise, because the one who truly experiences pain is the one being punished. A parallel to both is your saying: "Your day is fasting" (nahāruka sa'im), and "his grandfather's grandfather prospered" (jadda jaddahu).

**The chiefs (al-Mala')**: the word is from their saying "so-and-so is *mali'* with such-and-such," meaning he is capable of it. They are called *mala'* because they are "filled" with the competence for affairs, and they take them up and manage them. Or it is because they support one another (*yatamala'un*, i.e. they back and lean on each other). Or because they fill hearts with awe and assemblies with dignity [[His words "and assemblies with dignity" (*majalis abbah*), like *sakrah*, mean greatness. (ʿA.)]]. Or because they are full of wisdom and sound opinions. ﴿We do not see you but as a human like ourselves﴾ is an allusion (*taʿrid*) that they are more worthy of prophethood than he is. [[Mahmud said: "It is an allusion that they were more worthy of prophethood than he was... etc." Ahmad said: In both of these readings it may be intended to mean "first opinion." But the hamza was dropped because it is heavy to pronounce, unless the reader pronounces it with a *ya'* and does not hold to the view of softening the hamza. The two meanings are close. These people claimed to refute Noah with those who followed him on two grounds. The first: that the followers were the lowly, who are neither models nor examples. The second: that they had not even reflected before following him, and had not considered carefully whether what he brought was true, but had hurried into it without thought or deliberation. The aim of these people was that no proof should be established against them that some of them had believed him and affirmed him. And God knows best.]] And that God, had He willed to send down [this] to someone among humans, would have sent it to them. So they said: Suppose you are one of the chiefs and equal to them in rank, what made you more worthy than them? Do you not see their saying: ﴿and we see no superiority of yours over us﴾? Or they meant that it should have been a king, not a human being.

**The lowly (al-Arādhil)** is the plural of *al-arhal*, like the saying ﴿the greatest of its criminals (*akābira mujrimīhā*)﴾, meaning "the best of you in character." It is also read *bādi' al-ra'y* with and without the hamza, meaning: they followed you at first opinion or apparent opinion. Its position is adverbial of time. Its original form is: at the time when their first opinion arose, or at the time when their apparent opinion arose. That was omitted and the genitive noun was placed in its position. They meant: their following of you is only something that came to them immediately, without reflection or consideration. They regarded the believers as lowly because of their poverty and their lagging in worldly means, for they were ignorant and ﴿knew only an outward appearance of the life of this world﴾. So in their eyes the more honored was the one who had status and wealth, just as you see most of those who call themselves Muslims believing this and basing their honoring and dishonoring of people upon it. They have strayed far from realizing that advancement in this world does not bring anyone near to God but distances him, and does not raise him but lowers him, let alone make it a cause for being chosen for prophethood and qualified for it. Moreover, the prophets, peace be upon them, were sent to encourage seeking the Hereafter and renouncing the world, to make people disinclined to it, to belittle its status and the status of those who cling to it. How far their condition is from being characterized by what distances one from God, and from being honored by what is lowliness in God's sight.

**Any superiority (min faḍl)**: any increase of nobility over us that would qualify you for prophethood. **Rather, we think you are liars (bal nazunnukum kādhibīn)**: in what you claim.

Tell me, if I am upon a clear proof (bayyina) from my Lord, and He has given me a witness from Himself to attest to the truth of my claim, and has bestowed on me mercy from His presence, through granting me the clear proof. The clear proof in itself is the mercy. It is also permissible that by "clear proof" he means the miracle, and by "mercy" prophethood. If you say: the phrase "then it was made obscure to you" (fa-'ummiyat) is clear on the first interpretation, but what is its sense on the second? Ought it not to say "fa-'ummiyata" (in the dual)? I say: the sense is that the verb is understood as "fa-'ummiyat" after "clear proof," and its omission is for the sake of mentioning it only once. The meaning of "'ummiyat" is "was concealed" (khafiyat). It has also been read as:

"fa-'ummiyat" in the sense of "akhfiyat" (were hidden). In the reading of Ubayy: "fa-'amma-hā 'alaykum" (he made it obscure to you). If you say: what is its real meaning? I say: its real meaning is that the proof, just as it was made a source of insight and illumination, was made blind, because the blind man neither finds the way nor guides another. So the meaning of "it was made obscure to you" is that the proof was obscured and did not guide you, just as when the guide of a people is blinded in a desert, they remain without a guide. If you say: what is the meaning of Ubayy's reading? I say: the meaning is that they were resolute in turning away from it, so God left them (fa-khallāhum Allāh) to their resolve. That leaving was made into obscuring by Him. The evidence for this is His saying: "Shall we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?" That is, shall we force you to accept it and compel you to be guided by it, while you dislike it and do not choose it? "There is no compulsion in religion." Both object pronouns have been brought as attached pronouns together. It is also permissible for the second to be detached, as in your saying: "anulzimukum iyyāhā" (shall we impose it upon you). Similar to this is His saying: "So God will suffice you against them" (fa-sayakfīkahumu Allāh), and it is permissible to say: "fa-sayakfīka iyyāhum." It is related from Abu 'Amr that he pronounced the mīm with sukūn. Its basis is that the vowel was only a slight, fleeting sound, so the narrator took it to be a sukūn. But a clear sukūn is a grammatical error (laḥn) according to al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and the expert Basrans, because dropping the i'rab (grammatical inflection) vowel is permissible only in cases of poetic necessity. The pronoun in His saying "I do not ask you for it" (lā as'alukum 'alayhi) refers to His saying to them: "I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but God." It has been read: "wa-mā anā biṭārid alladhīna āmanū," with tanwīn, according to the original form. If you say: what is the meaning of His saying "indahum mulāqū rabbihim" (they will meet their Lord)? I say: its meaning is that they will meet God, and He will punish whoever drove them away; or they will meet Him, and He will reward them for the sound and firm faith in their hearts, as it appeared to me from them, and I know nothing other than that about them.

Or it refers to the opposite of that, which you attribute to them, such as building their faith on first opinion without reflection and contemplation. [Qawluhu "dhālika mimmā tuqarrifūnahum bihi," ay turmūnahum wa-tu'ībūnahum (i.e., you accuse them and find fault with them), as conveyed by al-Ṣiḥāḥ.]

And it is not for me to probe their hearts and to discover the secret of that from them, so that I should drive them away if the matter is as you claim.

Similar to this is His saying: "And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord" (al-Ans'am 52). Or they are believers in the meeting with their Lord, certain of Him, knowing that they will surely meet Him. "You are ignorant" (tajhalūn): you behave foolishly toward the believers and call them the lowest, from the saying of:

"Ala lā yajhalan aḥadun 'alaynā... fa-najhala fawqa jahli al-jāhilīna"

(Let no one act with ignorance toward us, lest we respond with greater ignorance than that of the ignorant.)

This is from the Mu'allaqa of 'Amr ibn Kulthum. "Ala" is an opening particle conveying emphasis, and "lā" is a prohibitive. The nūn is for emphasis of the prohibition. That is: let no one behave foolishly toward us and initiate evil against us. "Najhal" is in the subjunctive governed by an implied "an" after the fā' of causation, since it follows a prohibition. The requital of ignorance is called ignorance by way of figurative correspondence (mushākala), that is: we will repay him beyond his action against us, or beyond the ignorance of every ignorant person, and in addition to it.

Or "you are ignorant" of the meeting with your Lord. Or you are ignorant that they are better than you.

"Who will help me against God?" (man yanṣurunī mina Allāh), meaning: who will protect me from His vengeance, if I drive them away? They had been asking him to drive them away so that they might believe in him, out of disdain at being on equal footing with them.

"Nor do I know the unseen" (a'lamu al-ghayb) is conjoined to "I do not say I have the treasuries of God" (ʿindī khazā'inu Allāh). That is, I do not say: "I have the treasuries of God," nor do I say: "I know the unseen." The meaning is: I do not tell you, "I have the treasuries of God," so that I claim superiority over you in wealth, such that you would deny my superiority by your saying: "We see no superiority of yours over us" (wa-mā narā lakum 'alaynā min faḍl). Nor do I claim knowledge of the unseen, so that you accuse me of lying and fabrication, or until I become aware of what is in the souls of my followers and the inner thoughts of their hearts. "Nor do I say I am an angel," so that you say to me: "You are only a human like us." And I do not judge, concerning those whom you despise among the believers because of their poverty, that God will never give them any good in this world or the next because of their lowliness before Him, as you say. This is out of assistance to you and yielding to your desires. "Indeed, then I would be among the wrongdoers" (innī idhan la-mina al-ẓālimīn), if I said any of that.

"Al-izdirā'" (contempt) is an iftiʿāl form from "zarā 'alayhi," when one finds fault with him. "Azrā bihi" means: he belittled him. It is said: "izdarathu 'aynuhu" and "iqtaḥamathu 'aynuhu" (his eye looked down on him and passed over him with disdain).

"You have argued with us and you have greatly argued with us" (jādaltanā fa-akthartā jidālanā). The meaning is: you intended to argue with us, and you began it and made it abundant, like your saying: "Jād fulān fa-akthar" and "Aṭāb fa-akthar" (so-and-so was generous and abundant; so-and-so was good and abundant).

"Then bring us what you threaten us with, of the hastened punishment" (fa'tinā bimā ta'iduna min al-'adhāb al-mu'ajjal).

The requital of ignorance is called ignorance by way of figurative correspondence (mushākala), that is: we will repay him beyond his action against us, or beyond the ignorance of every ignorant person, and in addition to it.

Or "you are ignorant" of the meeting with your Lord. Or you are ignorant that they are better than you.

"Who will help me against God?" (man yanṣurunī mina Allāh), meaning: who will protect me from His vengeance, if I drive them away? They had been asking him to drive them away so that they might believe in him, out of disdain at being on equal footing with them.

Nor do I claim knowledge of the unseen, so that you accuse me of lying and fabrication, or until I become aware of what is in the souls of my followers and the inner thoughts of their hearts. "Nor do I say I am an angel," so that you say to me: "You are only a human like us." And I do not judge, concerning those whom you despise among the believers because of their poverty, that God will never give them any good in this world or the next because of their lowliness before Him, as you say. This is out of assistance to you and yielding to your desires. "Indeed, then I would be among the wrongdoers" (innī idhan la-mina al-ẓālimīn), if I said any of that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 33–35:

﴿Only Allah will bring it upon you﴾ meaning: the bringing of the punishment is not up to me; it is only up to Him, whom you have disbelieved in and disobeyed, ﴿if He wills﴾, meaning: if His wisdom requires that He hasten it for you. Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) read: "fa-akthartu jidalana" (so you have argued with us much). If you ask: what is the reason for the juxtaposition of these two conditions?

[Al-Zamakhshari quotes the gloss of Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir): "If you say: what is the reason for the juxtaposition of these two conditions... etc." Ahmad said: A parallel to this verse among the jurists' issues is the statement of one who says: "You are divorced if I drink, if I eat." This is what is titled the issue of the condition interposing on a condition (iʿtirāḍ al-sharṭ ʿala al-sharṭ).

What is transmitted from the Shafiʿis is that if she drinks and then eats, he does not break the oath; and if he eats and then drinks, he breaks it. This distinction is based on making the consequence belong to the other condition, that is, the one following it, and then making both together the consequence of the middle condition. There is a secret of Arabic grammar behind this which we will not lengthen by mentioning, and on this basis al-Zamakhshari parsed this verse as you have seen, and Allah knows best.]

I say: His saying ﴿if Allah wills to misguide you﴾ has as its consequent what is indicated by His saying ﴿my counsel will not benefit you﴾, and this indicating element stands in the position of what it indicates, so it is joined to a condition, just as the consequent is joined to the condition in your saying: "If you do good to me, I will do good to you, if I am able." If you ask: then what is the meaning of His saying ﴿if Allah wills to misguide you﴾?

[The question and its answer are based on the Muʿtazila doctrine that Allah does not create evil. As for the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, the "misguiding" (ighwāʾ) is on its apparent meaning: the creation of error (ghayy), that is, straying, in the heart. (ʿ)]

I say: When Allah knows from the unbeliever his persistence, He leaves him to himself and does not compel him; this is called misguiding and leading astray. Just as when He knows of him that he will repent and turn back, He shows him kindness: this is called guidance and direction. It was also said that ﴿an yughwiyakum﴾ means: that He destroy you, from "ghawa al-fasīl ghawā," when the suckling calf overfills and dies. Its meaning is: since you are, in your determination upon disbelief, at a level where Allah's counsels, admonitions and all His kindnesses do not benefit you, how would my counsel benefit you?

﴿Then upon me is my crime﴾: "ijrāmī" is in the form of a verbal noun and a plural, like His saying: "Allah knows their secrets (isrārahum) and their secrets (asrārahum)," and like: jurm and ajrām, qufl and aqfāl. The plural is supported by the fact that the earlier exegetes explained it as "my sins" (āthāmī). The meaning: if it is established and proven that I have fabricated it, then upon me is the punishment for my crime, that is, my fabrication. In that case it would be incumbent upon me that you turn away from me and gang up against me. ﴿And I am innocent﴾, meaning: since that has not been proven, and I am innocent of it. The meaning of ﴿of what you commit as crime﴾ concerns your crime in attributing the fabrication to me; so there is no basis for your turning away and hostility.

[Al-Zamakhshari quotes the gloss of Ahmad (ibn al-Munayyir): "If you say: what is the reason for the juxtaposition of these two conditions... etc." Ahmad said: A parallel to this verse among the jurists' issues is the statement of one who says: "You are divorced if I drink, if I eat." This is what is titled the issue of the condition interposing on a condition (iʿtirāḍ al-sharṭ ʿala al-sharṭ).

What is transmitted from the Shafiʿis is that if she drinks and then eats, he does not break the oath; and if he eats and then drinks, he breaks it. This distinction is based on making the consequence belong to the other condition, that is, the one following it, and then making both together the consequence of the middle condition. There is a secret of Arabic grammar behind this which we will not lengthen by mentioning, and on this basis al-Zamakhshari parsed this verse as you have seen, and Allah knows best.]

I say: His saying ﴿if Allah wills to misguide you﴾ has as its consequent what is indicated by His saying ﴿my counsel will not benefit you﴾, and this indicating element stands in the position of what it indicates, so it is joined to a condition, just as the consequent is joined to the condition in your saying: "If you do good to me, I will do good to you, if I am able." If you ask: then what is the meaning of His saying ﴿if Allah wills to misguide you﴾?

[The question and its answer are based on the Muʿtazila doctrine that Allah does not create evil. As for the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, the "misguiding" (ighwāʾ) is on its apparent meaning: the creation of error (ghayy), that is, straying, in the heart. (ʿ)]

I say: When Allah knows from the unbeliever his persistence, He leaves him to himself and does not compel him; this is called misguiding and leading astray. Just as when He knows of him that he will repent and turn back, He shows him kindness: this is called guidance and direction. It was also said that ﴿an yughwiyakum﴾ means: that He destroy you, from "ghawa al-fasīl ghawā," when the suckling calf overfills and dies. Its meaning is: since you are, in your determination upon disbelief, at a level where Allah's counsels, admonitions and all His kindnesses do not benefit you, how would my counsel benefit you?

﴿Then upon me is my crime﴾: "ijrāmī" is in the form of a verbal noun and a plural, like His saying: "Allah knows their secrets (isrārahum) and their secrets (asrārahum)," and like: jurm and ajrām, qufl and aqfāl. The plural is supported by the fact that the earlier exegetes explained it as "my sins" (āthāmī). The meaning: if it is established and proven that I have fabricated it, then upon me is the punishment for my crime, that is, my fabrication. In that case it would be incumbent upon me that you turn away from me and gang up against me. ﴿And I am innocent﴾, meaning: since that has not been proven, and I am innocent of it. The meaning of ﴿of what you commit as crime﴾ concerns your crime in attributing the fabrication to me; so there is no basis for your turning away and hostility.

﴿Never will believe﴾ is a despairing of their faith, and that it is like the impossible, to which no expectation attaches, ﴿except those who have already believed﴾, meaning, except those from whom what was expected of their faith has already occurred; "qad" here is for expectation, and "qad" has struck its mark. ﴿So do not be distressed﴾, meaning, do not grieve with the grief of one who is wretched and humbled. He said:

*Whatever God apportions, accept it without being distressed by it,*
*and sit as a noble man, of easy mind.* [[Labid? Hassan. It is said: ibtaasa (ابتأس) when one grieves from the frequent occurrence of misfortunes and hardships upon him. Al-bal (البال) is the heart or the state of affairs. He says: whatever God apportions to you of blessing or affliction, accept it while you are not grieved by it, that is, by what God has apportioned to you. And sit noble, not humiliated, good of condition and state, or at rest of heart from the toil of the world. And it is narrated: "wa-uq'ud" with a hamza cut (أقعد), from the transitive aqʻada, so that "karIman" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) according to the first, and an object according to the second, and in it there is tajrīd.]]

The meaning: do not grieve over what they have done of denying you, harming you and opposing you, for the time has come for your vindication over them. ﴿Before Our eyes﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: make it preserved, and its reality is: accompanied by Our eyes, as if God has eyes with him, guarding him lest he deviate in his crafting from what is correct, and lest any of his enemies come between him [[The phrase "and lest any of his enemies come between him" is perhaps: "and lest he come between." (ʿ)]] and his work. ﴿And Our revelation﴾: We reveal to you and inspire you how to make it. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him:

He did not know how to build the ship, so God revealed to him that he should make it like the breast of a bird.

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have done wrong﴾, meaning, do not call upon Me regarding your people, seeking to repel the punishment from them through your intercession. ﴿Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾: they are sentenced to drowning, and that has been decreed, the decree has been determined and the pen has dried, so there is no way to withhold it, like His saying: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾

It is narrated that Nuh (peace be upon him) built the ship over two years. Its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height was thirty cubits. It was made of teak wood, and he made it with three decks. He carried in the lowest deck the wild animals, beasts of prey and creeping creatures; in the middle deck the beasts and livestock; and he and those with him rode in the upper deck, along with what they needed of provisions. He also carried with him the body of Adam (peace be upon him), placing it across between the men and the women.

It is related from al-Hasan: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred.

It has also been said that the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said to ʿIsa (peace be upon him): "If only you would send us a man who witnessed the ship, so he could tell us about it." He said, "This is Kaʿb ibn Ham."

[[His saying "he chooses disbelief, not because He decreed it upon him" is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) that the decree and predestination do not precede evil and that He does not will it; but the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) is that every possible thing is preceded by decree, predestination and will, even if it is evil. (ʿ)]] Al-Dahhak said: he meant his son and his wife.

﴿Except a few﴾. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They were eight: Noah and his family, his three sons, and their wives." [[I have not seen it traced to the Prophet. Al-Tabari mentioned it with a chain from Qatadah, who said: "It was related to us that none were aboard the ship except Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their wives. So all of them were eight."]] It is also reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "They were ten: five men and five women." It was also said: they were seventy-two men and women, and Noah's sons were Sam, Ham and Japheth, along with their wives. So the total is seventy-eight: half of them men and half women.

It is permissible that this be one statement or two statements. The one-statement reading: that bismillah (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ) be joined to ﴿embark﴾ as a circumstantial clause from the waw (the plural subject), meaning: embark in it, invoking the name of God, or saying "In the name of God" at the time of its sailing and at the time of its anchoring. This is either because the "sailing" (majra) and the "anchoring" (mursa) are time-expressions, or because they are verbal nouns like "the sailing" (al-ijra') and "the anchoring" (al-irsa'), from which the temporal noun has been omitted, as in the expressions khafuq al-najm (the setting of the star) and muqaddam al-hajj (the arrival of the pilgrim).

It is also permissible that majraha (مَجْراها) and mursaha (مُرْساها) be taken as place-expressions for the sailing and anchoring, and their accusative case governed by the verbal sense contained in bismillah, or by the notion of saying contained in it. The two-statement reading: that bismillah be a separate nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) of subject and predicate, abrupt (muqtadabah), meaning: "In the name of God is its sailing and its anchoring." It is reported that when he wished it to sail, he said "In the name of God," and it sailed; and when he wished it to anchor, he said "In the name of God," and it anchored.

It is also permissible that the noun (ism) be superfluous (muqhamm), as in the verse:
[[Ibn Rabi'ah's...]] ... 

[Translator's note inserted by the commentary text: the poem follows.]

It is also permissible that the noun be superfluous, as in this line:

﴿Then peace be upon you both (ismu al-salam ʿalaykumā)﴾ [[My two daughters wish that their father would live, and am I anything but of Rabi'ah or Mudar?
If a day comes when your father dies, then do not scratch faces, nor shave hair.
And say: he is the man who neither abandons his friend, nor betrays the trusted one, nor is treacherous.
Peace be upon you both until the year is complete; and whoever weeps for a full year has made his excuse.]]

This is by Labid ibn Rabi'ah al-Amiri, advising his two daughters, Asma' and Yusrah. "Tamanna" (wished) is a past verb, or a present verb with one of its two taa's omitted; the interrogative is one of denial and is a metaphor for the certainty of death. "Yawman" (a day) is an adverbial complement of "hana" (came). "Murad bihi" means unrestricted time. "An yamūt" (that he dies) is the subject. "Khamasha wajhahu khamshan" means he wounded it with his nails; i.e., do not overdo your grief to the point of doing that. "Shi'ran" is in the accusative, placed in the form of the nominative by one dialect; he forbade them from grief and then commanded them after his praise of himself. "Sadiquhu" is a fronted object; "ila al-hawl" is attached to "qala." The word "ism" is superfluous between "thumma" and the word "al-salam," because he intended to greet them with this specific word, even though other words give the same meaning. It was said: he inserted it as a sign that there is no security for them after his death. In "thumma" there is an indication that he had not yet given peace, and that this would only be after the year; the meaning is that it does not occur to their minds, nor do they grieve for him after that. He expressed it by the peace of farewell, which entails separation, and separation customarily entails the absence of remembrance. It is also possible that the intention is to indicate that the bequest is complete. Then he said: "Whoever weeps over his affliction for a full year has made a strong excuse," as if he excuses his silence by saying he has discharged what was upon him; that is, "and you two are likewise."

And it is meant: ﴿by God is its sailing and its anchoring﴾, meaning by His power and His command. It was also read majraha wa-mursaha with a fatha on the mim, from "jara" and "rasa," either as verbal nouns, or as times, or as places. Mujahid read majriha wa-mursiha, with the active participle, in the genitive case, as two attributes of God. If you ask: "What is the meaning of your saying 'a muqtadabah sentence'?" I answer: its meaning is that Noah, peace be upon him, commanded them to board, then informed them that its sailing and its anchoring are by the mention of God's name, or by His command and power. It is possible that it is not muqtadabah, but in the position of a circumstantial clause, as in the verse:

﴿And they came to us with them drunk against us﴾ [[And they came to us with them drunk against us, so the people were routed, and the drunkard became sober.
"Al-sukr" and "al-sakr" are like "al-bu'd" and "al-ba'd." "Bihim sakr" is a circumstantial clause. "Alayna" is attached to "sakr," meaning: the people came to us in anger against us, and they withdrew from the place of battle and departed from it. The circumstance is that the drunkard among them was intoxicated by his drunkenness. It is reported as "fa-ajla al-yawm," meaning it passed and ended, or the darkness of battle was lifted on that day: that is, they did not remain except him, while the one who had been drunk was sober from his drunkenness, knowing that he was not fit for that. Here "ajla" is intransitive.]]

So it is not a self-standing statement, but a complement from the complements of the first statement. The accusative of this circumstantial clause refers to the pronoun of the ship, as if it were said: "Board it, its sailing and anchoring being [enacted] by God's name," meaning in the sense of the estimate (taqdir), like His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ (ud'khulūhā bi-salāmin āminīn). ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: were it not for His forgiveness of your sins and His mercy toward you, He would not have saved you.
