If you ask: "What is the response (jawab) of kullama (كلما)?" I answer: you are faced with two options. Either you make sakhirû (سَخِرُوا) the response and qala (قالَ) a resumptive new clause (isti'naf), on the assumption of a questioner's question; or you make sakhirû a substitute (badal) for marra (مَرَّ) or a qualifier (sifah) of mala' (مَلَأٌ), and qala the response.

﴿And your family﴾ is conjoined to "the two" (ithnayn), and likewise ﴿and those who believed﴾, meaning: carry your family and the believers from among others.

He excepted from his family the one against whom the word had already gone forth, that he is among the people of the Fire. The word had gone forth against him only because He knew that he would choose disbelief, not because He had decreed it upon him or willed it for him, exalted is God above that. [[His saying "he chooses disbelief, not because He decreed it upon him" is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) that the decree and predestination do not precede evil and that He does not will it; but the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) is that every possible thing is preceded by decree, predestination and will, even if it is evil. (ʿ)]] Al-Dahhak said: he meant his son and his wife.

﴿Except a few﴾. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "They were eight: Noah and his family, his three sons, and their wives." [[I have not seen it traced to the Prophet. Al-Tabari mentioned it with a chain from Qatadah, who said: "It was related to us that none were aboard the ship except Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their wives. So all of them were eight."]] It is also reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq: "They were ten: five men and five women." It was also said: they were seventy-two men and women, and Noah's sons were Sam, Ham and Japheth, along with their wives. So the total is seventy-eight: half of them men and half women.

It is permissible that this be one statement or two statements. The one-statement reading: that bismillah (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ) be joined to ﴿embark﴾ as a circumstantial clause from the waw (the plural subject), meaning: embark in it, invoking the name of God, or saying "In the name of God" at the time of its sailing and at the time of its anchoring. This is either because the "sailing" (majra) and the "anchoring" (mursa) are time-expressions, or because they are verbal nouns like "the sailing" (al-ijra') and "the anchoring" (al-irsa'), from which the temporal noun has been omitted, as in the expressions khafuq al-najm (the setting of the star) and muqaddam al-hajj (the arrival of the pilgrim).

It is also permissible that majraha (مَجْراها) and mursaha (مُرْساها) be taken as place-expressions for the sailing and anchoring, and their accusative case governed by the verbal sense contained in bismillah, or by the notion of saying contained in it. The two-statement reading: that bismillah be a separate nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) of subject and predicate, abrupt (muqtadabah), meaning: "In the name of God is its sailing and its anchoring." It is reported that when he wished it to sail, he said "In the name of God," and it sailed; and when he wished it to anchor, he said "In the name of God," and it anchored.

It is also permissible that the noun (ism) be superfluous (muqhamm), as in the verse:
[[Ibn Rabi'ah's...]] ... 

[Translator's note inserted by the commentary text: the poem follows.]

It is also permissible that the noun be superfluous, as in this line:

﴿Then peace be upon you both (ismu al-salam ʿalaykumā)﴾ [[My two daughters wish that their father would live, and am I anything but of Rabi'ah or Mudar?
If a day comes when your father dies, then do not scratch faces, nor shave hair.
And say: he is the man who neither abandons his friend, nor betrays the trusted one, nor is treacherous.
Peace be upon you both until the year is complete; and whoever weeps for a full year has made his excuse.]]

This is by Labid ibn Rabi'ah al-Amiri, advising his two daughters, Asma' and Yusrah. "Tamanna" (wished) is a past verb, or a present verb with one of its two taa's omitted; the interrogative is one of denial and is a metaphor for the certainty of death. "Yawman" (a day) is an adverbial complement of "hana" (came). "Murad bihi" means unrestricted time. "An yamūt" (that he dies) is the subject. "Khamasha wajhahu khamshan" means he wounded it with his nails; i.e., do not overdo your grief to the point of doing that. "Shi'ran" is in the accusative, placed in the form of the nominative by one dialect; he forbade them from grief and then commanded them after his praise of himself. "Sadiquhu" is a fronted object; "ila al-hawl" is attached to "qala." The word "ism" is superfluous between "thumma" and the word "al-salam," because he intended to greet them with this specific word, even though other words give the same meaning. It was said: he inserted it as a sign that there is no security for them after his death. In "thumma" there is an indication that he had not yet given peace, and that this would only be after the year; the meaning is that it does not occur to their minds, nor do they grieve for him after that. He expressed it by the peace of farewell, which entails separation, and separation customarily entails the absence of remembrance. It is also possible that the intention is to indicate that the bequest is complete. Then he said: "Whoever weeps over his affliction for a full year has made a strong excuse," as if he excuses his silence by saying he has discharged what was upon him; that is, "and you two are likewise."

And it is meant: ﴿by God is its sailing and its anchoring﴾, meaning by His power and His command. It was also read majraha wa-mursaha with a fatha on the mim, from "jara" and "rasa," either as verbal nouns, or as times, or as places. Mujahid read majriha wa-mursiha, with the active participle, in the genitive case, as two attributes of God. If you ask: "What is the meaning of your saying 'a muqtadabah sentence'?" I answer: its meaning is that Noah, peace be upon him, commanded them to board, then informed them that its sailing and its anchoring are by the mention of God's name, or by His command and power. It is possible that it is not muqtadabah, but in the position of a circumstantial clause, as in the verse:

﴿And they came to us with them drunk against us﴾ [[And they came to us with them drunk against us, so the people were routed, and the drunkard became sober.
"Al-sukr" and "al-sakr" are like "al-bu'd" and "al-ba'd." "Bihim sakr" is a circumstantial clause. "Alayna" is attached to "sakr," meaning: the people came to us in anger against us, and they withdrew from the place of battle and departed from it. The circumstance is that the drunkard among them was intoxicated by his drunkenness. It is reported as "fa-ajla al-yawm," meaning it passed and ended, or the darkness of battle was lifted on that day: that is, they did not remain except him, while the one who had been drunk was sober from his drunkenness, knowing that he was not fit for that. Here "ajla" is intransitive.]]

So it is not a self-standing statement, but a complement from the complements of the first statement. The accusative of this circumstantial clause refers to the pronoun of the ship, as if it were said: "Board it, its sailing and anchoring being [enacted] by God's name," meaning in the sense of the estimate (taqdir), like His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ (ud'khulūhā bi-salāmin āminīn). ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: were it not for His forgiveness of your sins and His mercy toward you, He would not have saved you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 42–43:

If you ask: To what does His saying ﴿and it sails with them﴾ connect? I answer: It connects to an omitted element indicated by ﴿Embark therein, in the name of God﴾, as if it were said: "So they embarked therein, saying, 'In the name of God,' and it sails with them," meaning: it sails while they are in it. ﴿Amid waves like mountains﴾ means the waves of the Flood. Each wave is likened to a mountain in its massing and height.

If you ask: The *mawj* (wave) is what rises above the water when it is agitated and surging [[His saying "when it is agitated and surging": in al-Sihah, "the valley surged" means it extended greatly and rose. From this one says "a surging sea" (bahr zakhir).]]. The water had met and covered what lay between heaven and earth, and the ships were running within the water as a fish swims. So what is the meaning of their sailing within the waves?

I answer: That was before the covering, and before the Flood had overwhelmed the mountains. Do you not see the saying of his son: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾? It was said: the name of his son was Kan'an. It was also said: Yam.

He (Ali, may God be pleased with him) recited *ibnaha* (her son), the pronoun referring to his wife. Muhammad ibn Ali and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr recited *ibnahu* with a fatha on the ha', meaning *ibnaha*, and they relied on the fatha in place of the alif. This supports the view of al-Hasan.

Qatada said: "I asked him, and he said, 'By God, he was not his son.' I said: 'God has related of him that "my son is of my family," and you say he was not his son, and the People of the Book do not differ that he was his son.' He said: 'And who takes his religion from the People of the Book?'" He argued from the saying ﴿of my family﴾, where He did not say "of me." As for his being attributed to his mother, there are two possibilities. One is that he was a stepson to him, like Umar ibn Abi Salama to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The other is that he was not of legitimate birth. This is a disgrace from which the prophets, peace be upon them, were protected.

Al-SudDi recited *wa nada Nuhun ibnaho* (and Noah called to his son), in the mode of lamentation and grief, meaning: he said, "O my son!"

*Al-Ma'zal* is a noun of place (*maf'al*), from *'azalahu 'anhu* when he moved him away and distanced him. The meaning is: he was in a place where he isolated himself from his father and from the ship of the believers. It was also said: he was in isolation from his father's religion.

*Ya Bunayya*: it was recited with a kasra on the ya', as an abbreviation of the ya' of possession. With a fatha, it is an abbreviation of the alif that replaces the ya' of possession, as in your saying *ya bunaya*. Or the ya' and the alif may have been dropped because two sukuns met, since the ra' after them is sukun.

﴿Except for him on whom God has mercy﴾: except the one who is merciful, namely God, the Exalted [[Mahmud said: "The intended meaning is 'except the one who is merciful, namely God,' or 'there is no protector today...' etc." Ahmad said: The possible readings are four: "there is no protector except one who is merciful," "no one protected except one who is shown mercy," "no protector except one who is shown mercy," and "no one protected except one who is merciful." The first two are an exception from the same category (*istithna' muttasil*, connected exception), and the other two are from a different category (*istithna' munqati'*, disconnected exception). Al-Zamakhshari added a fifth, "no protector except one who is shown mercy," considered to be of the same category through an interpretation involving the omission of the annexed noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*), its meaning being: "there is no place of a protector except the place of one who is shown mercy." The negation is an allusion to the non-protection of the mountain, and the affirmation is an allusion to the protection of the ship. All of these are permissible, and some are closer than others, and God knows best.]], or: there is no protector today from the Flood except one whom God has shown mercy to. That is, except the place of those believers whom God has shown mercy. ﴿And he was for them forgiving and merciful﴾ is in His saying ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. That is because when he made the mountain a protector from the water, it was said to him: "Today no protector will protect you from the mountain or anything like it, except one protector, which is the place of those whom God has shown mercy to and delivered, meaning the ship."

It was also said: *la 'asim* means *la dha 'ismatin* (no one having protection) except the one God has shown mercy to, like His saying ﴿of gushing water﴾ and ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (where the adjective is used in the sense of the one who has it).

It was also said: *illa man rahima* is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), as if it were said: "But whoever God has shown mercy to is the one protected." This is like His saying ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption﴾.

It was recited *illa man rahima* with the passive voice.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 44:

The address to the earth and the sky with what is addressed to one who discerns (al-hayawan al-mumayyiz) [[He (Mahmud) said: "The address to the earth and the sky with what is addressed to the rational being... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Of this pattern is the omission of mention of the described subject, being satisfied with its attributes, because it is singled out by them; and also the omission of the attributes at times, being satisfied with mention of the described subject, since it is made distinct by them and unique in them, and that whenever it is mentioned in their place, they are mentioned by its mention, as in His saying: ﴿And He is God in the heavens and in the earth﴾, the verse.

And the meaning is: He is God, the one described by the attributes of perfection, famed for them among the worlds. And from it is:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry."

Poets have indeed resorted to clinging to the hems of these subtle meanings. Abu al-Tayyib said, praising 'Adud al-Dawla:

"Do not praise yourself, but praise the lord (hammam), since no one who praises can name anyone but you."

He means: do not confer praise upon yourself, for you are the one singled out for praises; so when you are mentioned and the meaning is not named by them, no one else's mind is led to them, because of your singularity in them.]] with the wording of specification and turning to them in address from among all created things, which is His saying: ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾. Then He commanded them with what is commanded to people of discernment and reason, in His saying: ﴿Swallow your water﴾ and ﴿Withhold﴾, indicating great power, and that the heavens, the earth and these great bodies are submissive to His creation, in which He wills whatever He wills, not resisting Him. It is as if they were discerning rational beings who have known His greatness, majesty, reward, punishment and power over everything capable, and who have understood the necessity of obeying Him and submitting to Him; they fear Him and are alarmed at hesitating to comply with Him and to descend to His will immediately, without delay. So as His command reaches them, the commanded thing is accomplished without restraint or slowness. "Al-bal'" (swallowing) is an expression for drying up. "Al-iqla'" is holding back. One says: the rain ceased (aqla'a al-matar) and the fever ceased (aqla'at al-hummaa). ﴿And the water was diminished﴾: from "ghaad'a," when one reduces it. ﴿And the matter was decided﴾ and what God had promised Noah of the destruction of his people was fulfilled. ﴿And it settled﴾, the ship came to rest and stabilized ﴿on al-Judi﴾, which is a mountain near Mosul. ﴿And it was said: "Away!"﴾ One says "ba'ada, ba'dan wa bu'dan" when they intend far distance, in terms of destruction and death and the like. For this reason it is specific to invoking evil, and its reports come in the passive verb form, to indicate majesty and grandeur, and that such great matters occur only by the act of a capable agent and the formation of an overpowering creator, and that its doer is one agent who has no partner in his acts. So the mind does not go to someone else saying: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," nor that anyone other than Him decrees that tremendous matter, nor that the ship would come to rest upon the back of al-Judi and settle on it except by His arranging and establishing it. And because of the meanings and subtleties we have mentioned, the scholars of eloquence (ulama al-bayan) have deemed this verse most eloquent and have shaken their heads in admiration of it, not for the assonance of the two words, ﴿ub'li﴾ and ﴿aqli'i﴾; and that, though it does not leave the speech devoid of beauty, is like something not regarded in the presence of those beauties which are the core, while everything else is husk. From Qatada: the ship set sail with them on the tenth of Rajab, and it was on the water for one hundred and fifty days; it settled with them on al-Judi for a month, and they descended on the day of 'Ashura. It is narrated that it passed by the House (al-Bayt), circumambulated it seven times, and God had freed it from drowning. It is narrated that Noah fasted the day of the descent and commanded those with him, and they fasted in gratitude to God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 45–46:

"His calling out to his Lord" (nidā'ahu rabbahu): his supplication to Him, which is his saying ﴿My Lord﴾, together with what follows of demanding the fulfilment of His promise regarding the deliverance of his family.

If you say: since the calling out (al-nidā') is his saying ﴿My Lord﴾, how is ﴿and he said, "My Lord"﴾ conjoined to "called out" with the fa' (so-called fa' of consequence)?

I say: by "the calling out" is meant the intention to call out. Had the calling out itself been meant, it would have come without the fa', as in His saying ﴿When he called to his Lord with a secret call, he said: "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾ without a fa', meaning: some of my family, for he was his son from his loins, or he was his stepson, and so he is part of his family. ﴿And indeed Your promise is the truth﴾, meaning that every promise You make is the established truth, about which there is no doubt in its fulfilment and keeping. You promised me that You would deliver my family, so what of my son? ﴿And You are the most just of judges﴾.

That is, the most knowing of judges and the most just of them, because no judge has any superiority over another except through knowledge and justice. How many a drowned man in ignorance and oppression, among those who hold office in your time, has been given the title "the most just of judges" (aqḍā al-quḍāt)! Its meaning is "the most judicious of judges," so take heed and learn a lesson. It may also be that it derives from wisdom (ḥikmah), with ḥākim formed in the sense of having (nisba), as it is said "dāri' (armoured) from dir' (armour)," and "ḥā'iḍ" (menstruating) and "ṭāliq" (divorced) according to the view of al-Khalil. ﴿Indeed he is not of your family; he is an unrighteous deed﴾ — this is a reason for the negation of his being of his family. In it is an indication that kinship in religion overshadows kinship by lineage, and that your kinsman in your religion and creed is among the distant ones in rank, even if he is an Abyssinian and you are a Qurashi, close to you and specially chosen. And whoever does not share your religion, even if he is the closest of your relatives by blood, is the farthest of the far from you. He (God) made his very person "an unrighteous deed" as an exaggeration in censuring him, like the saying of the poet:

"For it is only approach and retreat."

[Note by the editor: the explanation of this witness has passed in the first part, page 218; refer to it if you wish.]

It is said: the pronoun refers to Noah's calling out, meaning: your calling out this is an unrighteous deed and not as it should be. If you say: why was it not said, "Indeed it is an corrupt deed"? I say: when He negated him from his family, He negated from him their attribute with the particle of negation by which the negated word remains, and this indicates that He delivered those of his family who were delivered only because of their righteousness, not because they were his people and your kin. Since righteousness was negated from him, his fatherhood did not benefit him, as in His saying ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, and those two availed them nothing against God﴾.

It is read: ﴿an unrighteous deed﴾, meaning: he did a deed that was not righteous. It is also read:

﴿So do not ask Me﴾ with the nūn kasrah without the ya' of the first person, and with the heavy nūn with a ya', and without a ya'; meaning: do not seek from Me a request or a seeking about which you do not know whether it is right or wrong, until you have grasped its reality. The mention of the matter is evidence that the calling out was before he was drowned, when he feared for him. If you say: why was his calling called a question when there is no question in it? I say: his supplication contained the meaning of a question, though it was not explicitly stated, because when he mentioned the promise of the deliverance of his family at the time his son was about to drown, he was demanding its fulfilment. And to ask about what one does not know the reality of is ignorance and folly, and He admonished him not to return to that, nor to the like of such deeds of the ignorant. If you say: He had promised him that He would deliver his family, and he did not know that his son was not of them in religion; when he was about to drown the matter became confused for him, because the promise had preceded for him, and he knew God to be wise, not permitting the doing of what is ugly or the breaking of a promise, so he sought the removal of the doubt, and seeking the removal of doubt is obligatory. Why then was he rebuked and his request called ignorance? I say: God, mighty and exalted, had first given him the promise of the deliverance of his family with the exception of those among them against whom the word had already gone forth. It was incumbent upon him to believe that among his family were those deserving of punishment because they were not righteous, that not all of them would be saved, and that no doubt should beset him, when his son was about to drown, that he was among the excepted and not among those excluded from the exception. So he was rebuked for being confused about what should not have been confused.

It may also be that it derives from wisdom (ḥikmah), with ḥākim formed in the sense of having (nisba), as it is said "dāri' (armoured) from dir' (armour)," and "ḥā'iḍ" (menstruating) and "ṭāliq" (divorced) according to the view of al-Khalil. ﴿Indeed he is not of your family; he is an unrighteous deed﴾ — this is a reason for the negation of his being of his family. In it is an indication that kinship in religion overshadows kinship by lineage, and that your kinsman in your religion and creed is among the distant ones in rank, even if he is an Abyssinian and you are a Qurashi, close to you and specially chosen. And whoever does not share your religion, even if he is the closest of your relatives by blood, is the farthest of the far from you. He (God) made his very person "an unrighteous deed" as an exaggeration in censuring him, like the saying of the poet:

"For it is only approach and retreat."

[Note by the editor: the explanation of this witness has passed in the first part, page 218; refer to it if you wish.]

It is said: the pronoun refers to Noah's calling out, meaning: your calling out this is an unrighteous deed and not as it should be. If you say: why was it not said, "Indeed it is an corrupt deed"? I say: when He negated him from his family, He negated from him their attribute with the particle of negation by which the negated word remains, and this indicates that He delivered those of his family who were delivered only because of their righteousness, not because they were his people and your kin. Since righteousness was negated from him, his fatherhood did not benefit him, as in His saying ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, and those two availed them nothing against God﴾.

It is read: ﴿an unrighteous deed﴾, meaning: he did a deed that was not righteous. It is also read:

﴿So do not ask Me﴾ with the nūn kasrah without the ya' of the first person, and with the heavy nūn with a ya', and without a ya'; meaning: do not seek from Me a request or a seeking about which you do not know whether it is right or wrong, until you have grasped its reality. The mention of the matter is evidence that the calling out was before he was drowned, when he feared for him. If you say: why was his calling called a question when there is no question in it? I say: his supplication contained the meaning of a question, though it was not explicitly stated, because when he mentioned the promise of the deliverance of his family at the time his son was about to drown, he was demanding its fulfilment. And to ask about what one does not know the reality of is ignorance and folly, and He admonished him not to return to that, nor to the like of such deeds of the ignorant. If you say: He had promised him that He would deliver his family, and he did not know that his son was not of them in religion; when he was about to drown the matter became confused for him, because the promise had preceded for him, and he knew God to be wise, not permitting the doing of what is ugly or the breaking of a promise, so he sought the removal of the doubt, and seeking the removal of doubt is obligatory. Why then was he rebuked and his request called ignorance? I say: God, mighty and exalted, had first given him the promise of the deliverance of his family with the exception of those among them against whom the word had already gone forth. It was incumbent upon him to believe that among his family were those deserving of punishment because they were not righteous, that not all of them would be saved, and that no doubt should beset him, when his son was about to drown, that he was among the excepted and not among those excluded from the exception. So he was rebuked for being confused about what should not have been confused.

"That I should ask You (ask You) in future for what I have no knowledge of its correctness, adopting the manners of Your discipline and taking admonition from Your admonition. And unless You forgive me (وَإِلَّا تَغْفِرْ لِي) for what has passed from me of that, and have mercy on me (وَتَرْحَمْنِي) by accepting my repentance, I shall be among the losers (﴿أَكُنْ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ﴾) in deeds."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 48:

It is read: "Yā Nūḥu ihbiṭ" (with the ba' pronounced with a damma, i.e. "ihbuṭ"), "bi-salāmin minnā" (with peace from Us), meaning safe and secured from Our side, or "musallaman ʿalayka mukarraman" (peace upon you, honored). "Wa-barakātin ʿalayka" and blessings upon you, "wa-mubārakan ʿalayka" (blessed upon you). Al-barakāt are the goods that increase and grow. It is also read "wa-barakatin" in the singular. "Wa-ʿalā umamin mimman maʿak" may take min here as explicative (lil-bayān), so that what is meant is the nations who were with him in the ship, since they were groups; or they are called umam because nations branch out from them. Or min may indicate the end point (li-ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), meaning: upon nations arising from those who are with you, and these are the nations until the end of time, and this is the more apparent view.

His words "wa-umamun" are in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject). "Sa-numattiʿuhum" is a descriptive clause (ṣifa), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted, its estimated form being: "wa-mimman maʿaka umamun sa-numattiʿuhum" (and among those who are with you are nations whom We shall provide for). It was omitted because His words "mimman maʿaka" indicate it. The meaning is: the peace is from Us and the blessings upon you and upon nations of believers who arise from those who are with you; and among those who are with you are nations given enjoyment of the world, who will be turned over to the Fire. Nūḥ, peace be upon him, was the father of the prophets, and creation after the Flood descended from him and from those who were with him in the ship.

It is related from Kaʿb ibn Muḥammad al-Qurazi:

Every believing man and woman until the Day of Resurrection entered into that peace, and in what follows of enjoyment and punishment, every disbeliever.

It is related from Ibn Zayd: "They descended, and by God He was pleased with them. Then He brought forth from them offspring, some of whom were shown mercy and some of whom were punished."

It has been said: the nations meant by "those given enjoyment" are the people of Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ and Shuʿayb.

This is a standard faithful rendering; I've kept the commentary's wording and transliterated the technical terms, with the Qur'anic quotation inside ﴿ ﴾.

"That" refers to the story of Noah (peace be upon him). Its place in the sentence is the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), and the clauses following it are its predicates (akhbar). That is: that story is among the news of the unseen (anba' al-ghayb) revealed to you, unknown to you and to your people, ﴿before this﴾ — before My revealing it to you and informing you of it. Or, ﴿before this﴾ means before this knowledge which you acquired through revelation. Or, ﴿before this﴾ means before this time. ﴿So be patient﴾ in conveying the message and in bearing the harm of your people, just as Noah was patient, and expect the outcome to be in your favour and in favour of those who denied you, similar to what befell Noah and his people. ﴿Indeed, the outcome is for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾ — in success, victory and triumph.

As for His words ﴿nor your people﴾, the meaning is: your people, among whom you live, despite their large numbers and great multitude, if this was not their state and they neither heard of it nor knew it, then how much more so [would be the case] for a single man among them. It is like saying: "This was not known to 'Abd Allah or to the people of his town."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 50–52:

Akhahum (their brother), wahidan minhum (one of them), and its accusative (intisab) is by coordination (ʿatf) upon "arsalna Nuhan" (We sent Noah). Hudan is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan). Ghayruhu in the nominative (raf') is an adjective (sifah) according to the place (mahall) of the prepositional phrase. It is also read ghayrihi in the genitive (jarr) as an adjective according to the wording (lafz): in ﴿in antum illa muftarun﴾ (you are only fabricators), "taftarun ʿala Allah al-kadhib" (you fabricate lies against God) by your taking idols as His partners. No messenger came except that he confronted his people with this statement, because their concern is sincere advice (nasihah), and sincere advice is not purified or made pure except by cutting off desires; and as long as any suspicion of them remains, it does not benefit or take effect. ﴿Afala taʿqilun﴾ (Will you not then reason?), for you reject the advice of one who seeks no wage for it except from God, which is the reward of the Hereafter, and nothing negates accusation more than that.

It was said: ﴿Istaghfiru rabbakum﴾ (Ask your Lord for forgiveness), believe in Him, ﴿thumma tubu ilayhi﴾ (then repent to Him) from worshipping other than Him, because repentance is not valid except after faith. Al-midrar means the one of abundant flow, like al-mighzar. He only intended to incline them towards faith and to encourage them to it by abundant rain and increased strength, because the people were owners of crops, gardens and buildings, intensely greedy for them, so they were most in need of water. They were boastful (mudillin) [[The phrase "wa kanu mudillin" is from al-dall. In al-Sihah: al-dall is close to al-huda, and both are from calm and dignity. (ʿ)]] with what they had been given of great strength, force, might and valour, protecting themselves thereby from the enemy, awe-inspiring in every direction. It was said: he meant strength in wealth.

It was also said: strength in sexual potency. And it was said: rain was withheld from them for three years and the wombs of their women became barren. From al-Hasan ibn ʿAli, may God be pleased with them both, that he delegated to Muʿawiyah; when he left, one of Muʿawiyah's attendants followed him and said: "I am a man of wealth and I have no children. Teach me something, perhaps God will grant me a son." He said: "Upon you is seeking forgiveness." So he would increase seeking forgiveness until he might seek forgiveness seven hundred times in one day, and he had ten sons. This reached Muʿawiyah, who said: "Why did you not ask him what he said that for?" So he delegated another delegation, and the man asked him, and he said: "Have you not heard the saying of Hud, upon him be peace, ﴿wa yazidkum quwwatan ila quwwatikum﴾ (and He will add strength to your strength), and the saying of Noah, upon him be peace, ﴿wa yumdidkum bi-amwalin wa banin﴾ (and He will provide you with wealth and children)?"

﴿Wa la tatawallaw﴾ (And do not turn away): do not turn away from Me and from what I call you to and what I encourage you towards, ﴿mujrimin﴾ (as criminals), persisting in your crimes and sins.

﴿Wa la tatawallaw﴾ (And do not turn away): do not turn away from Me and from what I call you to and what I encourage you towards, ﴿mujrimin﴾ (as criminals), persisting in your crimes and sins.

You came to us with no clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods merely on your word. We are not believers in you.

Commentary: "You have not brought us any clear proof": this is a denial and rejection on their part, just as the Quraysh said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?" along with the missing of the sign-verses being limited. "On your word" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "those who abandon our gods," as if it were said: "And we will not abandon our gods, departing from your word." "And we are not believers in you": it is not proper that people like us should believe someone like you in what he calls them to, despairing of his receiving a response.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 54–55:

"اعْتَراكَ" is the object (maf'ul) of "نقول" (we say); otherwise the clause would be meaningless (laghw). The meaning is: "We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil." That is, they have seized you and afflicted you with madness (junun) because you reviled them, turned away from them, and were hostile to them, as a retribution upon you from them for the evil of your deed, with an evil recompense. Therefore you speak the speech of madmen and rave with the raving of those afflicted with brisam (al-mubarsamin). [[The author's words "al-mubarsamin" in al-Sihah: "al-Barsam" is a known illness. (ʿ)]]

It is no wonder that those people call repentance and seeking forgiveness madness and insanity, for they are the leading banners of disbelief and the pillars of polytheism. What is truly wondrous is that there are people among those who openly profess Islam, whom we have heard calling the one who repents of his sins a madman and the one who turns in penitence to his Lord one afflicted with madness, while we do not find them, alongside that, to be even a tenth as affectionate as they were in the days of their ignorance. This is only because of a vein of atheism that refused except to throb, and a small dose of heresy (zandaqa) that wanted to raise its head. [[The author's words "wa-dabb min al-zandaqa" in al-Sihah: "al-Dabb" is resentment; and "al-Dabb" is one of the sprouts of the palm tree, which is its flower cluster. (ʿ)]]

The earlier replies of these people show that the people were coarse, hard-hearted, not caring for slander [[The author's words "la yubalun bil-buhtan": to attribute to a person what is not in him. (ʿ)] and not heeding advice, and their resolve did not yield to right guidance. This last point indicates extreme ignorance and utter stupidity, since they believed that stones could give victory and take vengeance. Perhaps, when they permitted punishment, they were also permitting reward.

It is among the greatest of signs that a single man confronts with these words a nation thirsting to shed his blood, shooting at him from one bow, and this is due to his trust in his Lord and that He protects him from them, so their claws do not sink into him. Nuh, peace be upon him, said something similar to his people: ﴿Then carry out your plan against me, and give me no respite﴾ (10:71). He affirmed his innocence of their gods and their polytheism, and strengthened it with what is customary among people, who confirm matters by the testimony of God and the testimony of His servants. A man says: "God is witness that I will not do such-and-such," and he says to his people: "Be witnesses that I will not do it."

If you ask: "Why was it not said: 'I call God to witness and I call you to witness'?" [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'I call God to witness and I call you to witness'... etc." Ahmad said: The summary of what he said is that the form of the statement does not admit anything other than reporting the occurrence of the testimony from him. Since his calling God as witness was a realized and certain fact, he expressed it in the form of a statement, because it is a valid and established testimony. And in addressing them he used the imperative form, which implies contempt for their religion and lack of concern for it, and this is his intent in this context with them. It is possible that his calling them to witness was real, and the purpose was to establish the proof against them. He turned from the form of the statement to the form of the imperative only to distinguish between his address to God Most High and his address to them, by expressing the address to God Most High in the form of a statement, which is more exalted and more dignified for the one addressed than the imperative form. And God is the One who grants success and the correct understanding.]] I say: Because calling God to witness of disavowal of polytheism is a valid and established testimony, in the sense of confirming monotheism and strengthening its bonds. As for their witnessing, it is nothing but contempt for their religion and an indication of little concern for them, merely. So he turned it away from the wording of the first, due to the difference between the two, and it was expressed in the wording of an imperative to bear witness, as a man says to one with whom the earth has dried up (i.e., one with whom he has no relationship): "Bear witness that I do not love you," mocking him and belittling his state.

﴿Of what you associate with Him﴾: of your associating gods with Him, or of what you associate as gods besides Him; that is, you make them partners to Him, while He has not made them partners. ﴿He has sent down no authority for that.﴾ ﴿So scheme against me, all of you together, you and your gods, as quickly as you can, without delay﴾, for I do not care about you or your scheming, and I do not fear your harm even if you cooperate against me, though you are the powerful and the strong. How then could your gods harm me, when they are only inanimate things that neither harm nor benefit? And how could they take revenge on me if I inflict harm upon them and turn away from worshipping them, by afflicting me and taking away my reason?

When he mentioned his reliance upon God and his confidence in His protection and guardianship against their plotting, he described Him by that which obliges reliance upon Him: that His lordship encompasses him and them, that every creature is in His grasp, under His possession and dominion, and under His subjugation and authority, and that He takes hold of their forelocks. This is an illustration of that: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, meaning that He is upon the path of truth and justice in His dominion, so that no wrongdoer escapes Him, and no one who seeks refuge in Him is lost before Him.

﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, if you turn away. If you ask: the conveying (of the message) took place before the turning away, so how did it come to be the response (jaza') to the condition? I say: its meaning is, "If you turn away, I am not to be blamed for any shortcoming in conveying (the message), and you are left without excuse, since what I was sent with has reached you, yet you refused anything but denying the message and opposing the Messenger." ﴿And He will bring in another people in your place﴾ is a new (independent) statement, meaning: God will destroy you and bring about a people who will succeed you in your homes and your wealth. ﴿And you will not harm Him at all by your turning away﴾, that is, not the least harm, because harm and benefit are not applicable to Him; rather, you harm only yourselves. Or (the meaning is): whoever is a watcher over all things, preserving them, while they are in need of His protection from harms, is not harmed by the like of you.

When he mentioned his reliance upon God and his confidence in His protection and guardianship against their plotting, he described Him by that which obliges reliance upon Him: that His lordship encompasses him and them, that every creature is in His grasp, under His possession and dominion, and under His subjugation and authority, and that He takes hold of their forelocks. And those who believed with him—it is said they were four thousand. If you ask: what is the meaning of repeating "deliverance"?

I answer: He first mentioned that when He destroyed their enemy, He delivered them, then He said, ﴿And We delivered them from a severe punishment﴾, meaning: that deliverance was from a severe punishment. That is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent upon them the simoom (samum, a scorching wind), which entered their noses and came out from their backsides, cutting them apart limb by limb. It is also said that by the second he meant deliverance from the punishment of the Hereafter, and there is no punishment more severe or more intense than it. And His saying, ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾, He means: by means of the faith which We favoured them with, granting them success in it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 59–60:

"And that was ʿĀd": a reference to their graves and their remains, as if he had said: "Travel through the earth, look upon them, and take heed." Then he resumed describing their state, saying: ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers﴾, because whoever disobeys his messenger has disobeyed all of God's messengers. ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾. It has been said that only Hud was sent to them alone. ﴿Every obstinate tyrant﴾, meaning their chiefs, their great ones, and their callers to the denial of the messengers.

The meaning of "following their command" is obeying them. Since they were followers of these men rather than of the messengers, curse was made to follow them in both abodes, overturning them upon their faces into the punishment of God. The repetition of "Alā" (Indeed/Surely) together with the summoning [of them] and the invocation against them on account of their disbelief is an amplification of their affair and an expression of its enormity, and an incitement to take heed from them and to beware of a state like theirs.

If you say: "Bu'dan" (Away with them) is an invocation for destruction, so what is the meaning of invoking it against them after their destruction? I say: its meaning is to indicate that they were deserving of it. Do you not see his saying:

*Brothers of mine, do not be far away forever...
And indeed, by God, they have gone far away.*

*How bitter is life after you...
Every life after you is wretched.*

*I wonder how you drink...
Indeed my drinking after you is a trickle.*

It is by Fatima bint al-Ahjam al-Khuza'iyya. The Arabs say: "bu'd" with a damma is the opposite of nearness, and with a kasra it means destruction; the present tense of the first is with a damma, and the present tense of the second is with a fatha. What is in the verse is from the first. "Mā amarra" is an exclamation of wonder. She likened life, which is living or that by which one lives, to something bitter, by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), and affirming bitterness is an imaginative representation (takhyīl); or she borrowed bitterness for deficiency by way of explicit metaphor (al-taṣrīḥiyya). "Al-nakad" is hardship, constriction, and disturbance. "Al-thamad" is a small amount of water with no source, so it quickly runs out; a man is called *mathmūd* when many requests for knowledge or wealth are made of him until what he has is exhausted. The meaning: her joy after them is cut off like a little water, and she expressed it thus to match what came before.

It is also related that after the first verse she said:

*Had their tribe been with them for a long time, even though they had been born for the acquisition of honour,*
*Some of the loss would have been lightened, or some of what I bear would have been lightened.*

*Every living thing, even if they multiply, is a bound-for watering place, and the basin to which they came is [the same].*

The meaning of "tamallatahum" is: they lived with them for a long span of time. The word "min" has been inserted with "ba'ḍ" being left without it, to indicate the intensification of hatred. The "mā" is superfluous, and "kull ḥayy" (every living thing) is an intensifier of generality. "Amarū" with a kasra means they multiplied. "Al-ḥawḍ" (the basin) is a metaphor for death.

﴿Of the people of Hud﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ʿĀd. If you say: what is the benefit of this clarification, and is the identification not achieved without it? I say: the benefit is that they be branded with this call and that a definite matter be established in them, free of any doubt in any respect. Also, ʿĀd are two ʿĀds: the first, the ancient one, which is the people of Hud and the story concerns them, and the other, Iram.

Not a young man is he who is not a source of light by which one is guided,
nor are there lasting traces of him upon the earth."

[[His words "bi-fataa" (a young man) are the predicate of "laysa" (is not). "Lā yustaḍāʾ bihi" (by whom one is not guided by light) is its qualifier. It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the first "al-fataa." He likened him, in good judgment and in guiding the one who seeks counsel, to a shining lamp. It is possible that he likened him to a star in the sky, to contrast it with the earth that follows. The common element is what has passed. It is also possible that the common element is that he removes the distress of poverty, just as the moon's light removes the darkness of night. It is reported that Muʿawiyah was asked: "Why did you increase the digging of rivers, the planting of trees, and the reviving of deserts?" He said: "Nothing moved me to it except this verse." "Al-āthār" (traces) are what he used to do. It is also possible that they are noble deeds that bring praise after death.]]

It has also been said: "istaʿmarakum" means "to make you long-lived," from "al-ʿumr" (life span), similar to "istabqākum" (to make you remain), from "al-baqāʾ" (remaining). This has also been derived from "al-ʿumrā" (a gift of life). There are two possible meanings. The first is that "istaʿmara" has the sense of "aʿmara," just as "istahlaka" has the sense of "ahlaka" (to destroy). Its meaning would be: He made you live long in your dwellings there, and then He will inherit them from you when your lifespans end. The second is that it means He made you people who inhabit your dwellings there, because when a man bequeaths his house to someone after him, it is as though he has given him its use for life, since he lives in it for his lifetime and then leaves it to another.

﴿Near, responsive﴾: near in mercy, easy to reach, and responsive to whoever calls upon Him and asks Him. ﴿Among us﴾: among ourselves. ﴿Hoped-for﴾: signs of goodness and indications of right guidance were showing in you, so we used to hope for you, that we might benefit from you, that you would be consulted in matters and asked for guidance in plans. When you spoke these words, our hope in you was cut off, and we knew that there was no good in you. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Excellent and good, we would put you before all of us." It has also been said: "We used to hope that you would join our religion and agree with us on what we are upon." ﴿What our fathers worshipped﴾ is a narration of a past situation. ﴿Doubt-inducing﴾: from "arābahu," when he caused him to fall into doubt, which is unease of the soul and the absence of tranquility that comes from certainty. Or it is from "arāba al-rajul" (the man became one who causes doubt), by metaphor of attribution (majāz ʿaqlī, a figure in which an action is attributed to something other than its real agent).

﴿If I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾: it has been said that the particle of doubt (in) is used, although he was certain that he was upon clear evidence, because his address was to the deniers. It is as though he said: Suppose that I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and that I am truly a prophet, and consider this: if I follow you and disobey my Lord in His commands, who will protect me from the punishment of God? ﴿Then you would only increase me, in that case, in loss﴾: that is, you would make my deeds lose value and nullify them. Or it means: what you say to me and what you impose on me would only increase me in making you lose, that is, in attributing to you ruin, and in telling you that you are lost.

﴿A sign﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), governed by the meaning of the verb contained in the demonstrative (hādhihi). If you ask: "What does ﴿for you﴾ relate to?" I say: to "āyah" as a preceding circumstantial clause, because if it had been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier of it. Since it came first, it took the accusative as a circumstantial clause. ﴿A near punishment﴾: an imminent one, which will not be delayed from touching you with harm except briefly. That was three days, after which it will fall upon you. ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your dwelling﴾: enjoy life in your land. The lands are called "diyār" (dwellings), because one is controlled (yudār) in them, that is, one acts freely. It is said "diyār Bakr" for their lands. The Arabs who live around Mecca say: "We are from the Arabs of the dwelling," meaning the Arabs of the region. It has also been said: in the dwelling of this world. It has also been said: they hamstrung her on Wednesday and perished on Saturday.

﴿Not to be denied﴾: not denied in it. The adverbial sense of time was extended by omitting the preposition and treating it like a direct object, as in the phrase "a witnessed day" (yawm mashhūd), from the verse:

And a day we witnessed [...]

[[And a day we witnessed, Sulaym and ʿĀmir, few in it, except the spear-thrusts that quench thirst.
He says: "And many a day we witnessed in it," so the preposition is omitted and the pronoun is attached to the verb, making the verb appear to take two objects: the first is the pronoun, and the second is "Sulaym," meaning their two tribes. "Few" is a qualifier of "day." "Its gains (nawāfil)" is its subject, and the scarcity of spoils is because his people do not guard their possession. Or the meaning is that his enemies gain nothing from his people except spear-thrusts, mocking them, so the exception is continuous. It is also possible that it is disconnected.

Describing a singular by a plural is considered in terms of its types or its ranks, so it is also plural. "Al-nahhāl" is the plural of "nāhil," meaning either full (rayyān) or thirsty (ʿaṭshān), by analogy here; so it is one of the words with opposite meanings. Describing the thrust as "nāhil" is a metaphor of attribution, because what is actually described as thirsty is the spear or the horseman. The meaning is that they relieve the rage of their hearts through that thrust.]]

Or it is a metaphor: as though it was said to the promise, "Fulfill with you," so when it is fulfilled it has been true and not false. Or it means a promise that is not false, since "al-makdhūb" (the false) is a verbal noun like "al-majlūd" and "al-maʿqūl," and like "al-maṣdūqah" with the sense of "truth."

﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾: it is read with the mīm (of yawmi'dhin) vowelled with a fatḥah, because it is attached to "idh," which is indeclinable, as in the verse:

At the time when I rebuked gray hair for my youth,

[[At the time when I rebuked gray hair for my youth, I said: "Why, I am still reformed, and the gray hair is a restraint."
This is by al-Nābighah al-Dhubyānī. The meaning is: I blamed myself in the time of gray hair for my youth, that is, for the inclination toward desire as young men do. His words "I said" explain the blame, that is: until now I have not woken from the intoxication of youth, while gray hair is restraining me from what calls for blame. The interrogative is reproachful, meaning that this should not be. "Wazzaʿtuhu" and "fa-ttaza'a" mean I restrained him and he refrained. The one who restrains (al-wāzi') is what puts the row in order and keeps it from crookedness. "Awzaʿanī" means he inspired me with what sets my affairs right.]]

If you ask: "What is it coordinated with?" I say: with "najjaynā" (We saved), because its implied meaning is "and We saved them from the disgrace of that day," as He said: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾. Being saved was from the disgrace of that day, that is, from its humiliation, its shame, and its exposure, and there is no greater disgrace than the disgrace of one whose destruction angers God and whose retribution is from Him. It is also possible that by "that day" He means the Day of Resurrection, just as the severe punishment has been explained as the punishment of the Hereafter.

It has been read ﴿Indeed Thamud﴾ and ﴿to Thamud﴾, both with tanwīn (nunation, the diptote-to-triptote distinction) and without it. Tanwīn is for the sense of the tribe or the great ancestor, and the absence of tanwīn is for definiteness and feminine form, in the sense of the tribe.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 69–73:

﴿Our messengers﴾ means the angels. Ibn ‘Abbas reported: Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him with two angels with him. It was also said: Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil. It was also said: they were nine. And from al-Suddi: they were eleven. ﴿With good news﴾ is the glad tidings of a son. It was also said: of the destruction of the people of Lut, but the apparent meaning is the son. ﴿Peace﴾: ﴿We greet you with peace﴾, ﴿peace﴾ [is] your [greeting], ﴿Peace﴾. It was also read: ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ [as] ﴿Salman﴾ ... He said, "Peace" [sallam], in the sense of salam. It was also said: salm and salam are like ḥarm and ḥaram, and he recited:

*We passed by and said, "Ayh, peace!" so she greeted [us],*
*As the clouds gleam with the lightning's shine, the glistening ones.*

[This is by Dhu al-Rumma Ghaylan ibn ‘Uqba. He says: we passed by the dwellings of the beloved Mayy, and we said, "Ayh," meaning, speak and be sociable. So we were given peace (salm), meaning safety and companionship. Then she greeted us, her front teeth gleamed and she quickly vanished, as the cloud gleams with the shine of lightning, and the lightning quickly vanished.

*Iktalla iktilālan* means it shone brightly. *Al-lawā'iḥ* means the apparent ones; it is an adjective of *al-ghamām* (the clouds), because it is plural in meaning.]

﴿And he did not delay in coming﴾: he did not delay in bringing it, but hastened it. Or: his coming was not delayed. *Al-‘ijl* is the calf of a cow. *Al-ḥasīl* and *al-khabash* are used in the dialect of the people of al-Sarāt, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) owned cattle. ﴿Roasted﴾ means cooked with *al-raḍf* (heated stones) in a trench, as in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. It was also said: ﴿roasted﴾ means dripping its fat, from *ḥanadhtu al-faras* when I put a saddle-cloth on the horse until it dripped with sweat, and this is supported by ﴿a fat calf﴾. It is said: *nakarahu*, *ankarahu* and *istankarahu* (to find strange/to disapprove), and *mankūr* is rare in their speech; likewise, "I deny you" (*ankarak*), but *munkar* and *mustankar* [are common]. Al-A‘shā said:

*She found me strange, and what she found strange*
*Among the events was nothing but grey hair and baldness.*

[This is by al-A‘shā. It is said *ankarahu* and *nakarahu*, meaning he did not know it and disliked it: the beloved did not recognise me, and what she found strange of the events was only grey hair and baldness, which is the recession of the hair on the head. It was also said: Abu ‘Ubayda heard Bashshār deny that this line belongs to al-A‘shā and say that it was fabricated and does not resemble his speech, and Abu ‘Ubayda marvelled at his acuity, as if his denial was confirmed in his view.]

It was said: he used to stay at the edge of the land, and he feared that they intended some harm to him. [Mahmud said: "It was said that he used to stay at the edge of the land and feared that they intended harm to him..." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: The story of Ibrahim appears in three places. This is the first, and it indicates that he felt fear of them only because he knew they were angels and did not know why they had come. The second is in al-Ḥijr, His saying: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim...﴾ up to ﴿Do not be afraid; we give you good news﴾. They did not reassure him by informing him that they were angels, but that they bring him good news, which shows that they sensed that he knew they were angels and was apprehensive about what they had come for. The third is in al-Dhariyat: ﴿So he felt apprehension of them. They said, "Do not fear," and gave him good news﴾, which is likewise. As for Lut, he did not perceive that they were angels until they informed him. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They said, "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will not reach you"﴾? So the first thing they informed him of was that they were messengers. The difference between this verse and the verses about Ibrahim is clear: Ibrahim knew that they were angels and Lut did not know it. It is not far-fetched, given Ibrahim's superiority over Lut, that his insight enabled him to know they were angels while Lut did not, peace be upon them both.]

It was also said: their custom was that if someone who came to them touched their food, they felt safe with him, and otherwise they feared him. The apparent meaning is that he sensed they were angels, and he disapproved of them because he feared that their coming was for a matter that God had disapproved of him for, or for the punishment of his people. Do you not see their saying: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾? This is said only to someone who knows them but does not know that they were sent. ﴿And he felt apprehension﴾ means he concealed it. [Mahmud said: "The meaning of *awjasa* is *aḍmara* (he concealed), and they only said 'do not fear' because they saw the trace of fear and change in his face..." Ahmad said: This interpretation is a mistake on the part of al-Zamakhshari, God knows best, because they only knew his fear and apprehension by his informing them of it. This is shown by His saying in another verse: ﴿He said, "Indeed we are apprehensive of you." They said, "Do not be apprehensive"﴾, and the story is the same, and God is the granter of success.] They only said "do not fear" because they saw the trace of fear and change in his face.

Or they recognised him through God's making him known to them. Or they knew that his knowledge that they were angels necessitated fear, because they used to descend only with punishment.

﴿And his wife was standing﴾: it was said: she was standing behind the curtain, listening to their conversation. It was also said: she was standing over their heads, serving them. In the codex of ‘Abdullah: ﴿and his wife was standing while he was sitting﴾. ﴿So she laughed﴾: out of joy at the removal of the fear. [Mahmud said: "And his wife laughed because she was delighted that the fear had gone..." Ahmad said: This interpretation is unlikely, because she said afterwards: ﴿"Woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and this my husband is an old man? Indeed this is a strange thing!"﴾. So if she had menstruated before the good news, she would not have marvelled, since there is nothing strange about the conception of one who menstruates; menstruation is customarily a sign that conception is possible. God is the granter of success.] Or [she laughed] at the destruction of the people of wickedness. Or her laughter was laughter of denial at their heedlessness, when the punishment had already overshadowed them. It was also said: she used to say to Ibrahim: "Take Lut, your brother's son, to you, for I know that a punishment will descend on these people," so she laughed with joy when the matter came as she had imagined. It was also said: she laughed, so she menstruated.

Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-A‘rabi read ﴿fa-ḍaḥikat﴾ with a fatḥa on the ḥā' [i.e., *ḍaḥikat* with fatḥa]. ﴿Ya‘qūb﴾ is in the nominative by being the subject (*raf‘ bi-l-ibtida'*), as if it were said: "And after Ishaq there is Ya‘qub, a child born or existing," that is, after him. It was also said: *al-warā'* means a grandson. It is reported from al-Sha‘bi that he was asked, "Is this your son?" and he said, "Yes, from *al-warā'*," and he was his grandson. It was read ﴿Ya‘qūb﴾ in the accusative (*naṣb*), as if it were said: "And We granted her Ishaq, and after Ishaq Ya‘qub," following the manner of his saying:

*... they are not reformers of a tribe,*
*Nor [one] who laments ...*

[The explanation of this evidence was given in the first part, page 381; refer to it if you wish. — its corrector.]

The *alif* in *yā waylatā* is substituted for the *yā'* of possession, and likewise in *yā lahfā* and *yā ‘ajabā*. Al-Hasan read *yā waylatī* with *yā'* according to the original form. ﴿Shaykhan﴾ is in the accusative, governed by what the demonstrative indicates. It was read *shaykh*, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This, my husband, is an old man," or *ba‘lī* is a substitute for the subject and *shaykh* is the predicate, or both may be predicates. It is said: she was given the good news when she was ninety-eight years old, and Ibrahim was one hundred and twenty. ﴿Indeed this is a strange thing!﴾: that a child should be born to two elderly people. This is a deeming-unlikely according to the custom that God has established. The angels disapproved of her wonder, so they said: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of God?﴾, because she was in the house of signs, the place of descent of miracles and matters that break customs, so it was incumbent upon her to be dignified and not to be impressed as other women are impressed who grew up outside the houses of prophethood. Instead of wonder, she should glorify and praise God. To this the angels, may God's blessings be upon them, pointed in their saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house﴾. They meant that this and similar things are bestowed upon you by the Lord of Might, and He singles you out for favour with it, O people of the house of prophethood, so it is not a matter for wonder. *Amr Allah* means His power and wisdom. His saying ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you﴾ is a new statement by which the denial of wonder is justified, as if it were said: "Beware of wonder, for the like of this mercy and blessing is abundant from God upon you." It was also said: the mercy is prophethood and the blessings are the tribes of the Children of Israel, since the prophets were from them, and all of them were descendants of Ibrahim. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾: doer of what deserves praise from His servants. ﴿Glorious﴾: generous, abundant in beneficence towards them.

*Ahl al-bayt* is in the accusative either as a vocative or by specification, because *ahl al-bayt* is praise for them, since what is meant is: the people of the house of the Friend of the Merciful.

It was also said: they were nine. And from al-Suddi: they were eleven. ﴿With good news﴾ is the glad tidings of a son. It was also said: of the destruction of the people of Lut, but the apparent meaning is the son. ﴿Peace﴾: ﴿We greet you with peace﴾, ﴿peace﴾ [is] your [greeting], ﴿Peace﴾. It was also read: ﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ [as] ﴿Salman﴾ ... He said, "Peace" [sallam], in the sense of salam. It was also said: salm and salam are like ḥarm and ḥaram, and he recited:

*We passed by and said, "Ayh, peace!" so she greeted [us],*
*As the clouds gleam with the lightning's shine, the glistening ones.*

[This is by Dhu al-Rumma Ghaylan ibn ‘Uqba. He says: we passed by the dwellings of the beloved Mayy, and we said, "Ayh," meaning, speak and be sociable. So we were given peace (salm), meaning safety and companionship. Then she greeted us, her front teeth gleamed and she quickly vanished, as the cloud gleams with the shine of lightning, and the lightning quickly vanished.

*Iktalla iktilālan* means it shone brightly. *Al-lawā'iḥ* means the apparent ones; it is an adjective of *al-ghamām* (the clouds), because it is plural in meaning.]

﴿And he did not delay in coming﴾: he did not delay in bringing it, but hastened it. Or: his coming was not delayed. *Al-‘ijl* is the calf of a cow. *Al-ḥasīl* and *al-khabash* are used in the dialect of the people of al-Sarāt, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) owned cattle. ﴿Roasted﴾ means cooked with *al-raḍf* (heated stones) in a trench, as in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. It was also said: ﴿roasted﴾ means dripping its fat, from *ḥanadhtu al-faras* when I put a saddle-cloth on the horse until it dripped with sweat, and this is supported by ﴿a fat calf﴾. It is said: *nakarahu*, *ankarahu* and *istankarahu* (to find strange/to disapprove), and *mankūr* is rare in their speech; likewise, "I deny you" (*ankarak*), but *munkar* and *mustankar* [are common]. *Among the events was nothing but grey hair and baldness.*

[This is by al-A‘shā. They did not reassure him by informing him that they were angels, but that they bring him good news, which shows that they sensed that he knew they were angels and was apprehensive about what they had come for. The third is in al-Dhariyat: ﴿So he felt apprehension of them. They said, "Do not fear," and gave him good news﴾, which is likewise. The difference between this verse and the verses about Ibrahim is clear: Ibrahim knew that they were angels and Lut did not know it. Al-Ruwʿ is what he had sensed of fear, when he denied (i.e., did not recognize) his guests. The meaning is: when his heart was reassured after fear, and he was filled with joy because of the good tidings replacing grief, he turned to the disputation. If you ask: where is the response (jawab) of "lamma" (when)?

I say: it is omitted, just as His saying "fa-lamma dhahabu bihi wa-ajmaʿu" (So when they took him away and agreed) has its response omitted; and His saying "yujadilunā" (he argues with Us) is a resumed statement indicating the response. Its estimated sense is: he became bold in addressing Us, or he perceived our disputation, or he said such-and-such.

Then he began, saying "yujadilunā fī qawmi Lūṭ" (he argues with Us concerning the people of Lot). It was also said that "yujadilunā" is itself the response of "lamma," and it came in the present tense to depict the situation as it was happening. It was also said that "lamma" turns the present tense into the sense of the past, just as "in" (if) turns the past tense into the sense of the future. And it was said: its meaning is "he began to argue with Us" and "he set about arguing with Us." The meaning is: he argued with Our messengers. His disputation with them was that they said: "Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town." He said: "Do you see, if there were fifty righteous men among its people, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." He said: "Then forty?" They said: "No." He said: "Then thirty?" They said: "No."

Until he reached ten. They said: "No." He said: "Do you see, if there were one Muslim man in it, would you destroy it?" They said: "No."

At that point he said: "Indeed, Lot is in it." They said: "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family." (The phrase) "fī qawmi Lūṭ" is in the sense of "concerning their people." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they said to him: "If there are five people who pray in it, the punishment will be lifted from them." And from Qatadah: "A people in which there are not ten, among whom is good" (the phrase "ʿashara fīhim khayr" – "ten among whom there is good" – is perhaps "ten who pray," [Editor's note: ʿ]). It was also said: there were four thousand thousand people in it.

Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing (ḥalīm), not hasty toward anyone who wronged him; ʾawwāh (sorrowful) was one who often lamented over sins; munīb (penitent) was one who turned back to Allah in what He loves and is pleased with. These attributes indicate tenderness of heart, compassion and mercy. So He made clear that this is what moved him to argue on their behalf, hoping that the punishment would be lifted from them and that they would be given respite, so that perhaps they would turn to repentance and return, just as it moved him to seek forgiveness for his father.
