It was also said that "yujadilunā" is itself the response of "lamma," and it came in the present tense to depict the situation as it was happening. It was also said that "lamma" turns the present tense into the sense of the past, just as "in" (if) turns the past tense into the sense of the future. And it was said: its meaning is "he began to argue with Us" and "he set about arguing with Us." The meaning is: he argued with Our messengers. His disputation with them was that they said: "Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town." He said: "Do you see, if there were fifty righteous men among its people, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." He said: "Then forty?" They said: "No." He said: "Then thirty?" They said: "No."

Until he reached ten. They said: "No." He said: "Do you see, if there were one Muslim man in it, would you destroy it?" They said: "No."

At that point he said: "Indeed, Lot is in it." They said: "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family." (The phrase) "fī qawmi Lūṭ" is in the sense of "concerning their people." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they said to him: "If there are five people who pray in it, the punishment will be lifted from them." And from Qatadah: "A people in which there are not ten, among whom is good" (the phrase "ʿashara fīhim khayr" – "ten among whom there is good" – is perhaps "ten who pray," [Editor's note: ʿ]). It was also said: there were four thousand thousand people in it.

Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing (ḥalīm), not hasty toward anyone who wronged him; ʾawwāh (sorrowful) was one who often lamented over sins; munīb (penitent) was one who turned back to Allah in what He loves and is pleased with. These attributes indicate tenderness of heart, compassion and mercy. So He made clear that this is what moved him to argue on their behalf, hoping that the punishment would be lifted from them and that they would be given respite, so that perhaps they would turn to repentance and return, just as it moved him to seek forgiveness for his father.

"Yā Ibrāhīm" (O Ibrahim), with an implied "saying": that is, the angels said to him, "Turn away from this disputation, even though compassion is your habit; there is no benefit in it. Indeed the command of your Lord has come," meaning His decree and judgment, which proceeds only from rightness and wisdom, and the punishment is descending upon the people without doubt. It cannot be averted by disputation, supplication, or anything else.

Lot's distress and the constriction of his resources [Note: his "constriction of his resources" (wa-ḍīq dhar‘ahu). In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: "One says ḍaqtu bi-l-amr dhar‘an (I was constricted by the matter, dhar‘an) when you cannot bear it and have no power over it. The root of dhar‘ is actually the extension of the hand, as if you mean: I extended my hand toward it but did not reach it." (ʿ)] was because he thought they were humans, and he feared for them the wickedness of his people and that he would be unable to resist and defend them against them. It is related that God, exalted is He, said to them: "Do not destroy them until Lot bears witness against them four times." When he walked with them, leading them to his house, he said to them: "Has not the report of this town reached you?" They said: "And what is their affair?" He said: "I bear witness by God that it is the worst town on earth in its deeds," saying this four times. They entered his house with him, and no one knew of it, but his wife went out and informed her people about them. It is said: "a difficult day" (yawm ʿaṣīb) and "ʿaṣaṣb," when it is severe, from your saying ʿaṣabahu, when he tied it tightly.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 78–79:**

﴿وَجَاءَهُ قَوْمُهُ يُهْرَعُونَ إِلَيْهِ وَمِن قَبْلُ كَانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ السَّيِّئَاتِ﴾ *yuhra'ūn* (they rush), *ka-annamā yudfa'ūn dafʿan* (as if they were being pushed forcibly). *Wa-min qablu kānū ya'malūna al-sayyi'āt* (and before this they used to commit evil deeds): that is, before that time they used to commit obscenities and multiply them, so they became accustomed to them and grew used to them, and their sense of their ugliness diminished. Therefore they came rushing, openly, with no shame restraining them. It was also said that the meaning is: Lot already knew their habit of committing obscenities before that.

﴿قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ هَٰؤُلَاءِ بَنَاتِي هُنَّ أَطْهَرُ لَكُمْ فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَلَا تُخْزُونِ فِي ضَيْفِي﴾ *Hā'ulā'i banātī* (these are my daughters): he wanted to protect his guests with his daughters, and that is the utmost of generosity. He meant: "These are my daughters, so marry them," and it was permissible for Muslim women to be married to disbelievers, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married his two daughters to ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab and Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ before the revelation, while they were both disbelievers. [[I say: the statement "Abu al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il" is a gross error; it is in fact Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ, and his name does not include "Wa'il." It seems his mind moved to al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, the father of ʿAmr, who has no part in this matter. As for the story of Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ's marriage to the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and likewise ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab, Ibn Ishaq mentioned it in al-Maghazi, and al-Tabarani related it by his chain, saying: Abu al-ʿAs ibn al-Rabiʿ was one of the men of Mecca in wealth and trustworthiness, and Khadijah was his maternal aunt. So Khadijah asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to marry him to Zaynab, and he would not oppose her. That was before he was sent with revelation. When God honored His Prophet (ﷺ) with prophethood, Khadijah and his daughters believed, but Abu al-ʿAs remained steadfast in his polytheism. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had married ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab to his daughter Ruqayyah. When he called the Quraysh to two matters, some of them said to others: "You have relieved Muhammad of his concern for his daughters, so return them to him." They went to Abu al-ʿAs, but he refused them. Then they went to ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab, and he divorced Ruqayyah, and they married him to the daughter of Saʿid ibn al-ʿAs. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan married her after him." He then mentioned the story of Abu al-ʿAs and his capture at Badr. Al-Bayhaqi also related in al-Dala'il, by way of Qatadah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) married his daughter Umm Kulthum in the pre-Islamic period to ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab, and Ruqayyah to his brother. When Islam came, Abu Lahab ordered his two sons to divorce the two daughters.]] It was also said that they had two obeyed leaders, so he wanted to marry his daughters to them. Ibn Marwan read *hunna atharu lakum* with the accusative (*hunna aṭhara*), and Sibawayh weakened it and said: "Ibn Marwan sat cross-legged in his grammatical error" (*iḥtabā ibn Marwān fī laḥnihi*). From Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla': whoever reads *hunna aṭharu* with the accusative has sat with his legs folded in his grammatical error (*tarabbaʿa fī laḥnihi*). The reason is that its accusative is to make it a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*, a state of the subject), in which the meaning of the verb is operative, as in His saying *hādhā baʿlī shaykhan* (this is my husband, an old man). Or *hā'ulā'* is in the accusative by a hidden verb, as if it were said: "Take these," and *banātī* is an apposition (*badal*), and this hidden verb governs the circumstantial accusative, and *hunna* is a separator (*faṣl*, a pronoun of separation). This is not permissible, because the separator is specific to occurring between the two parts of a sentence and does not occur between the circumstantial accusative and the element it qualifies. A possibility has been derived in which *hunna* is not a separator: that *hā'ulā'* is the subject (*mubtada'*), *banātī* is *hunna*, a sentence in the place of the predicate (*khabar*) of the subject, as in your saying *hādhā akhī huwa* (this is my brother, he), and *atharu* is a circumstantial accusative.

﴿فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ by preferring them over them. ﴿وَلَا تُخْزُونِ﴾ do not disgrace me or humiliate me or expose me, from *al-khizy* (disgrace). Or do not shame me, from *al-khazāyah*, which is shyness. ﴿فِي ضَيْفِي﴾ regarding my guests, for when a man's guest or neighbor is disgraced, the man himself is disgraced, and that is from the nobility of generosity and the genuineness of manliness. ﴿أَلَيْسَ مِنكُمْ رَجُلٌ رَّشِيدٌ﴾ is there not among you one man of sound judgment, who is guided to the path of truth and good deeds, and who restrains from evil? It was read: *wa-lā tukhzūn* (without the *yā'*).

It is also possible that offering his daughters to them was an exaggeration in his humility toward them and a display of his intense distress at what they had brought upon him, hoping that they would feel shame before him and show him mercy when they heard that, and so leave him his guests, given that the matter was evident and it was established knowledge with him and with them that there was no intermarriage between him and them. For this reason they said, ﴿قَالُوا لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ مَا لَنَا فِي بَنَاتِكَ مِنْ حَقٍّ﴾ calling upon his knowledge, "You know we have no right to your daughters," because you do not see marriage with us as lawful, and this was merely a fine garment offered as a gift (*ʿarḍ sābarī*). [[The phrase "ʿarḍ sābarī" (with a fatḥah on the ʿayn) is a type of thin cloth, attributed to Sabur, one of the Sasanian kings, as stated in a marginal note. In the Sihah: "ʿaraḍtu lahu al-shay'," meaning I showed it to him and presented it to him. One says: "I offered him a garment in place of his right." In the proverb: "ʿarḍ sābarī," because it is a fine garment bought with the first offer and not bargained over. (ʿ)]] It was also said: when they made the mounting of males their way and religion by agreement among themselves, they considered that to be the truth, and that marrying females was falsehood. Therefore they said, "We have no right at all to your daughters," because marrying females is a matter outside the way of life we are upon. It is also possible that they said this in a spirit of wantonness, while the aim was to deny desire. ﴿لَتَعْلَمُ مَا نُرِيدُ﴾ they meant the mounting of males, and what desire they had for it.

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, as in His saying ﴿And if a Qur'an were such that the mountains were set moving by it﴾ [13:31]. The meaning is: if I had strength against you, I would have done to you and acted (against you).

It is said: "I have no strength for it" (*ma li bihi quwwa*), and "I have no capacity for it" (*ma li bihi taqa*). Similar to this is His saying ﴿They have no power against them﴾ [27:37], and "I have no two hands for it" (*ma li bihi yadan*), because it means: "I cannot shoulder it and I cannot manage it alone."

The meaning is: "If I were strong enough against you by myself, or if I took refuge with a strong person to lean on, who would protect me with his strength and shield me from you." He compared the strong and mighty one to a rock (*rukn*) of a mountain in its firmness and its defence. For this reason the angels said, when they had perceived his distress: "Indeed, your rock is strong."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lot; he used to take refuge in a strong rock" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from a hadith of Abu Hurayra within a longer narration.]]

It is also recited as *aw awiya* (with a fatḥa on the *yā'*), with *an* (that) implied, as if it were said: "If that I had strength against you, or that I took refuge," like her saying:

*Lalbsu 'abā'atin wa taqarra 'aynī*
*Ahabbu ilayya min labsi al-shufūf*

*Labīs* (the first word) is in the genitive after the preposition in the line; the transmission *lalbus* (with *la-* as an emphatic particle beginning the line) as the subject is a distortion (*tahrīf*, altering of the text), though it is widely transmitted.

These two lines are by Maysūn bint Baḥdal al-Kalbiyya, mother of Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. Her heart was constricted by her life with Mu'awiya, and he said to her: "Today you are in a kingdom whose value you do not know, and before it you were in a cloak." She then said this. The meaning is: a tent (*bayt*) of hair in which the winds flutter is dearer to me than a lofty, elevated palace; *anāfa* (the verb of *ināfa*, "to rise high") means he rose. Some Arabs say *arwāḥ* as the plural of *rīḥ* (wind), out of fear of confusion with the plural of *rūḥ* (spirit), as *a'yād* is the plural of *ʿīd* (festival), out of fear of confusion with *ʿūd* (wood).

*Wa labsu* ("and wearing") is conjoined to what precedes it. The variant *lalbsu* as the subject is a distortion, even though it is common. *Labsu 'abā'a* means a coarse woollen cloak, and "my eye refreshed" (*qurrat 'aynī*) along with it means my joy. "Is dearer to me than wearing sheer garments and a heated, grieving eye." *Shufūf* is the plural of *shaff*, the thin cloth, as if it does not hide what is behind it. *Shaffa yashuffu shufūfan* means he became emaciated; *shaffa-hu yashuffu-hu* (with kasra) *shafan* means it made him emaciated.

It is also recited as *ilā rukn* with two *ḍammas*. It is narrated that when they (the messengers) came, he closed his door, began to turn them back, and argued with them, as Allah related about him. Then they scaled the wall.

When the angels saw what distress Lot had fallen into, they said: "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you turn around, except your wife..." (see the verse). "Verily, they shall not reach you" is a sentence explaining the one before it, for since they were messengers of God, they could not reach him or harm him.

It was read: "fa-asri" (فَأَسْرِ) with a cut (qat') and with a wasl (connected hamza). And "illa imra'ataka" (إِلَّا امْرَأَتَكَ) with raising (rafʿ) and with accusative (naṣb).

It is narrated that he said to them: "When is the appointed time of their destruction?" They said: "At dawn." He said: "I wish it were sooner than that." They said: "Is not the dawn near?" (ألَيْسَ الصُّبْحُ بِقَرِيبٍ). It was also read "al-subh" (الصبح) with two dammas.

If you ask: What is the reasoning of the one who reads "illa imra'ataka" in the accusative? I answer: he makes it an exception from His words "fa-asri bi-ahlika" (فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ). The proof of this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-asri bi-ahlika bi-qit'in mina al-layli illa imra'ataka" (فأسر بأهلك بقطع من الليل إلا امرأتك). It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as an object of "la yaltafit" (لا يلتفت), on the basic principle of exception, although the eloquent form is substitution (al-badal), namely the reading of the one who reads with raising, so that she is a substitute for "ahad" (أحد). Concerning her leaving with his family there are two reports. It is narrated that he brought her out with them, and commanded that none of them turn around except her. When she heard the sound of the punishment, she turned around and said: "O my people!" (يا قوماه), and a stone struck her and killed her.

And it is narrated that he was commanded to leave her behind with her people, for her inclination was toward them, so he did not travel with her. The difference between the two readings corresponds to the difference between the two reports.

We made its highest part its lowest. Jibril (Gabriel) placed his wing under its lowest part, then raised it up toward the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters. Then he overturned it upon them, and they were pursued by stones ﴿from sijjil﴾. It was said: sijjil is a word arabized (mu'arrab) from the Persian *sang-i-gil* (stone and clay). The evidence for this is His saying ﴿stones of clay﴾. It was also said: it derives from *arsala* (to send), because they are sent upon the wrongdoers, and the evidence for this is His saying ﴿that We may send upon them stones﴾. It was also said: it is from what God decreed to punish them with from the record (*sijjil*). The record belonged to a certain person, and ﴿layered﴾ means arranged in the sky in layers, prepared for punishment. It was also said that some of them were sent one after another in succession. ﴿Marked﴾ means marked for punishment. It is reported from al-Hasan that they were marked with white and red. It was also said that they bore a sign by which it could be known that they were not stones of the earth. It was also said: the name of each one to be struck by them was written upon it. ﴿And it is not far from any wrongdoer﴾. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah.

It is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he asked Jibril (peace be upon him)? He said: "He means the wrongdoers of your nation. None of them is except that he is in the path of a stone that will fall upon him from one hour to another." [[al-Tha'labi mentioned it from Anas without a chain of narration.]]

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the towns, meaning they are close to the wrongdoers of Makkah, who pass by them on their journeys. ﴿Not far﴾ means not distant at all. It is also permissible that it means: "and it is not in a far place," because although it is in the sky, which is a far place, once it falls from there it is the swiftest thing in reaching its target, so it is as if it were near to it.

It was also said that they bore a sign by which it could be known that they were not stones of the earth. It was also said: the name of each one to be struck by them was written upon it. ﴿And it is not far from any wrongdoer﴾. In this there is a warning to the people of Makkah.

It is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he asked Jibril (peace be upon him)? He said: "He means the wrongdoers of your nation. None of them is except that he is in the path of a stone that will fall upon him from one hour to another." [[al-Tha'labi mentioned it from Anas without a chain of narration.]]

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the towns, meaning they are close to the wrongdoers of Makkah, who pass by them on their journeys. ﴿Not far﴾ means not distant at all. It is also permissible that it means: "and it is not in a far place," because although it is in the sky, which is a far place, once it falls from there it is the swiftest thing in reaching its target, so it is as if it were near to it.

I see you have prosperity (bi-khayr), so let not your conduct deprive you of it. Or: I see you in a blessing from God whose due is to be met with other than what you do. Or: I see you in good, so do not remove it from yourselves by what you are doing, like the words of the believer of the family of Pharaoh: "O my people, to you belongs the dominion today, dominant in the land; but who will help us against the might of God should it come upon us?" (Qur'an 40:29). [Al-Zamakhshari's wording here is "bi-khayr", "bi-ni'mah", as above.]

Quranic quote: "Indeed I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day." (11:84)

"Muhit" (encompassing): from the same root as "wa-uhita bi-thamarihi" (and his fruit was encompassed), meaning destroying, from the encirclement of an enemy.

If you say: is describing the punishment as "encompassing" more eloquent, or describing the Day as such? I say: rather, describing the Day with it, because the Day is a time that contains events; when it encompasses its punishment, all of what it contains of it is gathered for the one being punished, just as when it encompasses his bounty.

If you say: the prohibition of deficiency is a command to give full measure, so what is the benefit of his saying "give full measure"? I say: they were first forbidden from the very wrong they were engaged in, namely shortchanging the measure and the scale, because stating the wrong explicitly is a rebuke and reproach to the one forbidden. Then the command to give full measure, which is good according to reason, came explicitly in its wording, to increase the inducement to it and to urge it. It was qualified with "with justice": i.e., let the giving be in a manner of justice and equality, without excess or deficiency, a command to what is obligatory, because what goes beyond justice is a surplus and a recommended matter. And in it is a stipulation that the one giving full measure should intend by it fulfilling with justice, because the reason the giving-full is good is that it is justice and fairness. So these are three benefits.

"Bakhs" (al-bakhs): diminution and deficiency. The term "bakhs" is also used for the maks (tax levied on goods). Zuhayr said:

"And in every sale a man makes, there is a bakhs of a dirham."

Some transmit: "Mak̲s dirham" (a dirham's tax). The people of Iraq used to do this in their markets with the Arabs and others, and Zuhayr said: this is not fitting. "Ala" is originally compounded of the interrogative hamza of reproach and the negating "la", and became a particle of urging. It is said "istahyā" and "istahā," as here, by moving the vowel of the yā to the ḥā and deleting it, meaning: let the kings be ashamed of us, and let them guard against the punishment of violating our sacred things and wealth, lest they guard against killing us in return for killing some of them.

It is also transmitted: "Ala yastahī minnā al-malīku wa-yuttaqā," and so on, where "al-malik" is a dialect form of "al-mulk," meaning the king of Iraq.

Some transmit "maks dirham," and they used to take from everything sold a portion, as brokers do. Or they used to levy taxes on people. Or they used to reduce the prices of what they bought, so they were forbidden from that. "Al-athy fi al-ard" is like theft, raiding and highway robbery. It is also permissible to make shortchanging and diminution a form of corruption on their part in the land.

"Baqiyyatu Allāh" (what remains of God's provision): what remains for you of the lawful, after abstaining from what is forbidden to you: "What remains with God is better for you, if you are believers" (11:86). Its meaning: if you are believers, on condition that you believe. They were addressed to abandon shortchanging, diminution and corruption in the land while they were disbelievers, on condition of faith.

If you say: "What remains of God is better for the disbelievers, since by it they are spared the consequence of diminution..." I say: this too is Zamakhshari's affirmation of the verse in its apparent sense.

Its benefit appears with faith, through gaining reward together with deliverance from punishment; its benefit is obscure without faith, since its possessor is immersed in the depths of disbelief.

In this is the magnification of faith and an alert to the greatness of its status. It is also permissible to mean: if you are confirming me in what I say to you and advise you with. It is also permissible to mean: what remains for you with God of acts of obedience is better for you, like His words: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord" (18:46). The attribution of "baqiyyah" to God is because it is His provision, which may be attributed to Him. As for the unlawful, it is not attributed to God and is not called provision. And if "baqiyyah" means obedience, it is like saying "obedience to God."

It is read "taqiyyat Allāh" with a tā', meaning His piety and watchfulness which turns one away from sins and ugly acts. "And I am not a guardian over you": I was not sent to keep account of your deeds and recompense you for them; I was sent only as a messenger, a warner, a guide to good, and an adviser, and I have given you full excuse by warning you.

Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) used to pray a great deal, and whenever his people saw him praying they would wink at one another and laugh. By their words "Does your prayer command you..." they intended mockery and derision. Although the prayer may be said to "command" in a figurative sense, just as it "forbids" in His words, ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾, and although it may be said that prayer commands what is good and right, just as one says "it calls to it and urges toward it," they framed their speech in the manner of taunting (al-tanz) [[On his phrase "in the manner of taunting": in the Sihah, al-tanz means mockery (al-sukhriyya). One says tanaza yatanizu, fa-huwa tannaz, and I think it is a later coinage or a loanword. (Ed.)]] and made the prayer the one issuing commands in a sarcastic way about his prayer. They meant that what he commanded them, namely abandoning the worship of idols, was false and had no valid basis, that no sound reason would call one to it and no discerning mind would order it. Nothing remained, they said, but that it was commanded by the babble and whispering of Satan, namely his prayers which he maintained by night and by day, which in their view belonged to the category of madness and of the things that madmen and the obsessed are fond of, from among certain sayings and actions. The meaning of ﴿does your prayer command you that we abandon﴾ is: "does your prayer command you, by way of imposing that we abandon..." [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is: does your prayer command you by imposing that we abandon what our fathers worship," up to his words "with the second-person ta' in both." Ahmad said: On this reading, ﴿an naf'ala﴾ is conjoined to ﴿an natruka﴾; but on the familiar reading this is not permissible, because the meaning would be impossible, so the conjunction must be to ﴿ma ya'budu﴾, as if they said: "does your prayer command you that we abandon the worship of our fathers, or the object of our fathers' worship," whether the particle is masdariyya or mawsula. Then they said: "or that we do" — i.e., "or that we abandon our doing with our wealth what we wish." This is a subtle point, so be alert to it. There is no need for al-Zamakhshari to posit an elided genitive, meaning "commands you by imposing that we abandon," and his argument for it, that a person is not commanded to do another's act, is a branch of the question of the creation of acts. Nevertheless, positing an elided noun in the verse is justified, not on the basis of the aforementioned reading, but because the convention of address in such a context requires it. And God knows best.]] ﴿what our fathers worshipped﴾. The noun "the imposition" (al-taklif) is elided, since a person is not commanded to do another's act. The reading ﴿aṣalātuka﴾ in the singular is also transmitted. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited ﴿aw an taf'ala fi amwalina ma tasha'﴾ with the second-person ta' in both places, and this is what he used to command them: to refrain from fraud and short-weighing, and to be content with a small lawful sustenance rather than a large unlawful one.

It is also said that he used to forbid them from clipping (ḥadhf) [[On his phrase "clipping the dirhams": in the Sihah, ḥadhaftu min sha'rī wa-min dhanab al-dabba means I took from my hair and from the tail of the animal. (Ed.)]] the dirhams and dinars and shaving them down. By their words ﴿indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ they meant to ascribe to him the utmost of foolishness and error, and they inverted the terms in order to mock him, as one mocks a miser whose stone does not even trickle, and it is said to him: "If Hatim saw you, he would prostrate to you." It is also said that the meaning is: "indeed you are the one famed among your people for forbearance and rectitude," meaning that what you command does not match your condition and the reputation for which you are known.

﴿And He has bestowed upon me from Him a good provision﴾: i.e., from His presence (min ladunhu), a good provision, which is what He gave him of prophethood and wisdom. It was also said: a good provision means lawful and pure, without diminishing (the measure) or cheating in weights and measures.

If you ask: where is the answer to "a-ra-aytum" (ara'aytum, "Tell me")? Why is it not stated, as it was in the story of Noah and Lot? I say: its answer is omitted. It was not stated because its being stated in the two stories indicates its place, and the meaning of the sentence calls for it.

The meaning is: "Tell me, if I am upon clear proof and certainty from my Lord, and I am truly a prophet, would it be proper for me not to command you to abandon the worship of idols and to refrain from sins? Are not prophets sent only for that?"

It is said: "Khalafani fulan ila kadha" (so-and-so opposed me toward such-and-such) when he intends it while you turn away from it; and "khalafani 'anhu" (he opposed me away from it) when he turns away from it while you intend it. Suppose a man meets you coming back from the water, and you ask him about his companion, and he says: "Khalafani ila al-ma'" (he went against me to the water), meaning that he has gone to it arriving, while I am departing from it returning. From this is His saying: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾, meaning: I do not intend to get ahead of you to the desires which I have forbidden you, so as to monopolize them without you.

﴿I intend nothing but reform﴾: I intend only to reform you by my admonition, my counsel, my commanding of what is right and forbidding of what is wrong.

﴿As far as I am able﴾: "ma" is a time adverb (zarf), meaning: for the duration of my ability. (Mahmud said: "ma istata'tu" is a time adverb, meaning: for the duration of my ability to reform, and as long as I am able to do so. It is permissible that it be by omission of a noun, its estimate being "illa al-islah islah ma istata'tu" (except the reform of what I am able to reform), or that it be an object of the verbal noun, as in his saying: "dhaif al-nikayati a'da'ahu" (weak in inflicting harm upon his enemies). Ahmad said: The apparent reading is that it is an adverb, as it is in His saying ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾. As for making it an object of the verbal noun, which has been defined by "al" (the definite article), that is far-fetched, because governing a definite verbal noun over an explicit object is not that common. They said: In the Qur'an there is no case of a verbal noun governing an explicit object or anything else except in His saying ﴿Allah does not love the public utterance of evil﴾, where he governed a prepositional phrase. Turning away from the sequence of i'rab (grammatical inflection) to its unmarked form is possible but obstinate; it is certainly preferable, especially in the most eloquent speech. And Allah knows best.) for reform, as long as I am able and not failing in it. Or it is an appositive to "reform", meaning: the amount of it that I am able to achieve.

It is also permissible that it be by omission of a noun, according to your saying: "illa al-islah islah ma istata'tu" (except the reform of what I am able to reform).

Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), as in his saying: "dhaif al-nikayati a'da'ahu" (weak in inflicting harm upon his enemies)
[Weak in inflicting harm upon his enemies, / He thinks fleeing will postpone his term.]
(Nakaa al-qarh: he reopened the wound after it had healed, by hamza; and nakaa al-'aduww nikayatan: he killed him or wounded him. "A'da'ahu" is the object of "al-nikaya". Governing a verbal noun preceded by "al" as here is rare. "Yakhal" means: he thinks that fleeing from the enemy will prolong his life because of his cowardice.)

That is: "I intend only to reform what of your corruption I am able to reform."

﴿And my success is only through Allah﴾: my being successful in hitting the truth in what I do and what I leave, and its occurring in accordance with the pleasure of Allah, is only by His help and support. The meaning is: he sought success from his Lord in carrying out the matter in its course, and asked Him for support and victory over his enemy. Implicit in this is a warning to the disbelievers and a cutting off of their hopes concerning him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 89–90:

"Jarama" (to commit, to earn) works like "kasaba" (to earn) in taking one object or two. You say: "jarama dhanban wa kasabahu" (he committed a sin and earned it), and "jaramtuhu dhanban" or "kasabtuhu iyyahu" (I caused him to earn it). The poet says:

*"I struck Abu 'Uyayna a blow... Fazara has earned after it that they should be angry."*

This is by Ziyadah ibn Asma'. It is said: "jarama dhanban" means he acquired a sin. "Jarama al-nakhl" means he cut the palm trees. "Jaramtuhu kadha" means I caused him to acquire it or made him bear it. The meaning is: I struck that Fazari man with a blow that killed him. "Jaramat Fazara" means that Fazara deserved anger after it, or that Fazara acquired anger after it only. The nominative reading for them is well known. But al-Jawhari said that "Fazara" is the first object, meaning: I made them deserve anger, or I caused them to acquire it, or I made them bear it so that they became angry after it. This is by dropping the preposition.

From this is His saying, ﴿Let not my dissension cause you to incur what befell...﴾, meaning: let not my opposition cause you to earn the punishment that befalls you.

Ibn Kathir read it with a damma on the yā' (yajrimannakum), from "ajramtuhu dhanban," meaning I made him a doer of it, that is, an earner. This is transferred from "jarama" when it takes one object, just as "akhsabahu al-mal" (he made him earn wealth) is transferred from "kasaba al-mal" (he earned wealth). Just as there is no difference between "kasabtuhu malan" and "akhsabtuhu iyyahu," there is no difference between "jaramtuhu dhanban" and "ajramtuhu iyyahu." The two readings are equal in meaning with no difference between them, except that the well-known reading is more eloquent in wording, just as "kasabtuhu malan" is more eloquent than "akhsabtuhu."

By eloquence is meant that it is more frequent on the tongues of the eloquent Arabs whose Arabic is trusted, and they use it more often. Abu Hayawa, and what is related from Nafi', read ﴿mithla ma asaba﴾ with a fatḥa, because it is attached to something not fully declinable, as in the poet's words:

*"Nothing prevented her from drinking except that a dove spoke... on a branch, a tree of some kind, or he said..."*

This is by Abu Qays ibn Ruqa'ah describing his she-camel. "Fiha" means in the abode of the beloved. "Al-wajna'" means the hard and strong [camel]. "Al-shamlal" means the light and swift. "Al-irqal" and "al-da'da'a" are two kinds of gait. He likened the concealment of the hills, which are small mountains, by the mirage, which is the shimmering white seen at midday that resembles water flowing over the ground, to being clothed, which is wearing garments, by way of explicit metaphor (al-tasrihiyya). Then he described her with keenness of heart, which is praised among them, or with her longing for her homeland, and her turning when she heard the dove's voice. "Al-shurb," with a kasra, is a share of water; with a ḍamma, it is the verbal noun. "Al-awqal" is the plural of "waql," like "jabal," and they are stones, or remnants left in the trunk of a tree after some of its branches were pruned, projecting so that one can climb on them. He says: he did not prevent her share of water from her, or did not prevent her from drinking water. In this there is inversion (qalb) in the second, and it is not the subject, because it is the one it is attached to that has been made dependent on it. It was built on fatḥa because it is attached to a built word. He borrowed the word "spoke" for the dove's warbling by way of explicit metaphor, as if she were inside the branches, so the she-camel heard her voice without seeing her and was startled. Or she was on a branch of the tree, so her warbling was pleasant and delightful, and the she-camel longed for her homeland. "Dhat aw qal" is a description of "ghuṣn," since it is the plural of "ghuṣn," as it is said of "falak," where the singular and plural are considered in terms of a hidden change.

It is permissible to read "ghuṣn" as attached to "dhat," and the meaning would be: a branch of land or a tree with a sort of [thing], but the first is better for the meter.

It is also related: "fi ghuṣūn dhat aw qal," meaning: having projecting pieces after pruning, so that its appearance is disfigured, which causes aversion and dread, or having stones, so that it is greener where it is seen as green in the midst of barren land. Or it may be that it is in a place other than its own, which causes the she-camel to long for its proper place or to be startled by the strangeness of that. It was said: it is the plural of "waql," with a sukūn, which is the doum-palm tree. It was said: it is permissible that it is from "waqala," like "wa'ada," when it means to ascend, that is, having elevations.

﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ means: they were destroyed in a time near to your time, so they are the nearest of the destroyed to you. "Jarama" (to commit, to earn) works like "kasaba" (to earn) in taking one object or two. You say: "jarama dhanban wa kasabahu" (he committed a sin and earned it), and "jaramtuhu dhanban" or "kasabtuhu iyyahu" (I caused him to earn it). The poet says:

*"I struck Abu 'Uyayna a blow... Fazara has earned after it that they should be angry."*

This is by Ziyadah ibn Asma'. It is said: "jarama dhanban" means he acquired a sin. "Jarama al-nakhl" means he cut the palm trees. "Jaramtuhu kadha" means I caused him to acquire it or made him bear it. The meaning is: I struck that Fazari man with a blow that killed him. "Jaramat Fazara" means that Fazara deserved anger after it, or that Fazara acquired anger after it only. The nominative reading for them is well known. But al-Jawhari said that "Fazara" is the first object, meaning: I made them deserve anger, or I caused them to acquire it, or I made them bear it so that they became angry after it. This is by dropping the preposition.

From this is His saying, ﴿Let not my dissension cause you to incur what befell...﴾, meaning: let not my opposition cause you to earn the punishment that befalls you.

Ibn Kathir read it with a damma on the yā' (yajrimannakum), from "ajramtuhu dhanban," meaning I made him a doer of it, that is, an earner. This is transferred from "jarama" when it takes one object, just as "akhsabahu al-mal" (he made him earn wealth) is transferred from "kasaba al-mal" (he earned wealth). Just as there is no difference between "kasabtuhu malan" and "akhsabtuhu iyyahu," there is no difference between "jaramtuhu dhanban" and "ajramtuhu iyyahu." The two readings are equal in meaning with no difference between them, except that the well-known reading is more eloquent in wording, just as "kasabtuhu malan" is more eloquent than "akhsabtuhu."

By eloquence is meant that it is more frequent on the tongues of the eloquent Arabs whose Arabic is trusted, and they use it more often. Abu Hayawa, and what is related from Nafi', read ﴿mithla ma asaba﴾ with a fatḥa, because it is attached to something not fully declinable, as in the poet's words:

*"Nothing prevented her from drinking except that a dove spoke... on a branch, a tree of some kind, or he said..."*

This is by Abu Qays ibn Ruqa'ah describing his she-camel. "Fiha" means in the abode of the beloved. "Al-wajna'" means the hard and strong [camel]. "Al-shamlal" means the light and swift. "Al-irqal" and "al-da'da'a" are two kinds of gait. He likened the concealment of the hills, which are small mountains, by the mirage, which is the shimmering white seen at midday that resembles water flowing over the ground, to being clothed, which is wearing garments, by way of explicit metaphor (al-tasrihiyya). Then he described her with keenness of heart, which is praised among them, or with her longing for her homeland, and her turning when she heard the dove's voice. "Al-shurb," with a kasra, is a share of water; with a ḍamma, it is the verbal noun. "Al-awqal" is the plural of "waql," like "jabal," and they are stones, or remnants left in the trunk of a tree after some of its branches were pruned, projecting so that one can climb on them. He says: he did not prevent her share of water from her, or did not prevent her from drinking water. In this there is inversion (qalb) in the second, and it is not the subject, because it is the one it is attached to that has been made dependent on it. It was built on fatḥa because it is attached to a built word. He borrowed the word "spoke" for the dove's warbling by way of explicit metaphor, as if she were inside the branches, so the she-camel heard her voice without seeing her and was startled. Or she was on a branch of the tree, so her warbling was pleasant and delightful, and the she-camel longed for her homeland. "Dhat aw qal" is a description of "ghuṣn," since it is the plural of "ghuṣn," as it is said of "falak," where the singular and plural are considered in terms of a hidden change.

It is permissible to read "ghuṣn" as attached to "dhat," and the meaning would be: a branch of land or a tree with a sort of [thing], but the first is better for the meter.

It is also related: "fi ghuṣūn dhat aw qal," meaning: having projecting pieces after pruning, so that its appearance is disfigured, which causes aversion and dread, or having stones, so that it is greener where it is seen as green in the midst of barren land. Or it may be that it is in a place other than its own, which causes the she-camel to long for its proper place or to be startled by the strangeness of that. It was said: it is the plural of "waql," with a sukūn, which is the doum-palm tree. It was said: it is permissible that it is from "waqala," like "wa'ada," when it means to ascend, that is, having elevations.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 91–95:

"Ma nafqahu" means: "We do not understand (ma nafhamu) much of what you say." They said this because they were not paying attention to him (lam yulqun ilayhi adhhanahum), out of aversion and dislike for him, like His saying ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾. Or they did understand it, but did not accept it, so it was as if they had not understood it. They said this in a manner of belittling him, as a man says to his companion when he pays no heed to his speech: "I do not know what you are saying." Or they regarded his speech as raving and confusion, from which little benefit could come to them. And how could his speech not benefit them, when he was the orator of the prophets? It was also said: he had a speech impediment (alta') among us, weak, having no strength or honour among us. [[Mahmud said: "The meaning of their saying 'weak' is: you have no strength and no honour among us... etc." Ahmad said: This is one of the finest subtleties indicating that he was accomplished in the science of eloquence (al-bayan). And God is the One sought for help.]] So you cannot prevent us if we intend you some harm. It is related from al-Hasan: "weak, humiliated." It was also said: "weak" means blind. The Himyarites call the blind person "weak," just as they call him "blind" (darir). But this is not sound, because "fina" (among us) rejects it.

Do you not see that if it were said, "We see you among us as blind," it would not be a meaningful statement, because the blind man is blind among them and among others. For this reason they belittled his people, calling them a "group" (rahṭ). The rahṭ is from three to ten. It is also said: up to seven.

They only said "and were it not for your people" out of respect for them and regard for them, because they were of their religion, not out of fear of their might and power: "we would have stoned you," meaning we would have killed you in the worst manner. "And you are not mighty against us," meaning you are not dear to us and not honoured, so that we would honour you by refraining from killing you and spare you from stoning. Rather, your people are dear to us, because they are of our religion; they did not choose you over us, nor did they follow you instead of us. The placing of his pronoun after the negative particle indicates that the statement is directed at the agent, not at the action, as if it were said: "You are not mighty against us; rather your people are the mighty ones against us." For this reason he replied to them: ﴿Is my people more dear to you than God?﴾. Had it been said, "You have not been made mighty against us," this reply would not be correct.

If you say: the statement concerns him and his people, and that they are the mighty ones for them rather than him, so how is his saying ﴿Is my people more dear to you than God?﴾ correct? I say: their disdain for him, who is the Prophet of God, is a disdain for God. So when his people were dear to them rather than him, his people became dearer to them than God. Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ and ﴿you have taken Him behind your backs﴾, meaning you have forgotten Him and made Him like a thing cast behind the back, not heeded. The "zhihriyy" is a relative form from "zahr" (back), and the kasra is one of the changes in relative forms. Its parallel is their saying in the relative of "amsi" (yesterday): "amsiyy."

﴿Surely my Lord encompasses what you do﴾: He has encompassed your deeds in knowledge, so nothing of them is hidden from Him. ﴿Act according to your station﴾: "makanah" may not be free of being in the sense of "makan" (place), as one says makan and makanah, maqam and maqamah; or it may be a verbal noun from makna, makanatan, so he is makin. The meaning: act while standing firm in your way in which you are, of polytheism and hatred of me; or act while empowered to be hostile to me, able to do so. ﴿I too am acting; you will soon know﴾, according to what God gives me of help and support. And ﴿who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾: it is permissible for "man" to be interrogative, suspended from the verb "to know" in its action on it, as if it were said: "You will soon know which of us will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and which of us is the liar." And it is permissible for it to be relative, with the verb acting on it, as if it were said: "You will soon know the wretched one to whom will come a punishment that disgraces him, and the one who is the liar."

If you say: what is the difference between inserting the fa' and omitting it in ﴿you will soon know﴾? I say: inserting the fa' is an overt connection through a particle established for connection; omitting it is a hidden, estimated connection through a resumptive statement that answers an assumed question. As if they had said: "What will happen when we act according to our station and you act?" So he said: "You will soon know." Thus he connected sometimes with the fa' and sometimes with resumption, for variety in eloquence, as is the custom of the eloquent Arabs. The strongest and most forceful of the two connections is the resumption, and it is one of the branches of the science of eloquence whose beauties are abundant. ﴿And watch, and I too am watching with you﴾: "watch" means await the outcome. And "raqib" means "one who awaits" (muntazir). Raqib may be in the sense of "one who watches" (raqib), from raqabahu, like "darib" and "sarim" in the sense of "dharib" and "sarim." Or in the sense of "murāqib" (one who observes), like "ʿashir" and "nadim." Or in the sense of "murtaqib" (one who anticipates), like "faqir" and "rafiʿ," meaning "muftaqir" and "murtafiʿ."

If you say: their action according to their station has been mentioned, and his action according to his station; then He followed it with mention of the outcome of the actors from him and from them. So the analogy would be to say: "one to whom will come a punishment that disgraces him, and who is truthful," so that "one to whom will come a punishment that disgraces him" refers to the deniers, and "who is truthful" refers to the Prophet sent to them. I say: the analogy is as you mention, but since they were calling him a liar, He said ﴿and who is a liar﴾, meaning in your opinion and claim, as a way of making them appear ignorant. If you say: why are the two stories of ʿĀd and of Madyan introduced with "and" (wa), while the two intermediate stories are introduced with "fa'"? I say: the two intermediate ones came after the mention of the promise, which is His saying ﴿Surely their appointment is the morning; that is a promise not to be denied﴾, so the "fa'" which signifies causation was used, as you say: "I promised him, and when the appointment came, such and such happened." As for the other two, they did not occupy that position; rather they came as independent beginnings, so it was right that they be joined by a conjunctive particle to what preceded them, as one story is joined to another story.

"Al-jathim": the one who remains in its place and does not move, like "al-labid" (the one pressed flat). It means that Gabriel cried out at them with a cry, so that the soul of each one of them departed, dead on the spot (qa'san), ﴿as if they had never dwelt there﴾: as if they had not remained in their homes alive, going and coming. "Al-bu'd" (distance) has the meaning of "al-bu'd," which is destruction, like "al-rushd" with the meaning of "al-rushd." Do you not see His saying ﴿as Thamud were destroyed﴾? Al-Sulami read "ba'idat" with a damma on the ʿayn; the meaning in both forms is one, and it is the opposite of nearness, except that they wished to make a distinction between distance in the sense of destruction and other than that, so they changed the pattern, just as they distinguished between the two verbs of good and evil, saying "wa'ada" and "awʿada." Al-Sulami's reading came in accordance with the original form, taking the meaning of distance without specification, as one says "dhahaba fulan wa-mada" with the meaning of death. It was also said: its meaning is "distance (bu'dan) for them from the mercy of God, as Thamud were distanced from it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 91–95:

"Ma nafqahu" means: "We do not understand (ma nafhamu) much of what you say." They said this because they were not paying attention to him (lam yulqun ilayhi adhhanahum), out of aversion and dislike for him, like His saying ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾. Or they did understand it, but did not accept it, so it was as if they had not understood it. They said this in a manner of belittling him, as a man says to his companion when he pays no heed to his speech: "I do not know what you are saying." Or they regarded his speech as raving and confusion, from which little benefit could come to them. And how could his speech not benefit them, when he was the orator of the prophets? It was also said: he had a speech impediment (alta') among us, weak, having no strength or honour among us. [[Mahmud said: "The meaning of their saying 'weak' is: you have no strength and no honour among us... etc." Ahmad said: This is one of the finest subtleties indicating that he was accomplished in the science of eloquence (al-bayan). And God is the One sought for help.]] So you cannot prevent us if we intend you some harm. It is related from al-Hasan: "weak, humiliated." It was also said: "weak" means blind. The Himyarites call the blind person "weak," just as they call him "blind" (darir). But this is not sound, because "fina" (among us) rejects it.

Do you not see that if it were said, "We see you among us as blind," it would not be a meaningful statement, because the blind man is blind among them and among others. For this reason they belittled his people, calling them a "group" (rahṭ). The rahṭ is from three to ten. It is also said: up to seven.

They only said "and were it not for your people" out of respect for them and regard for them, because they were of their religion, not out of fear of their might and power: "we would have stoned you," meaning we would have killed you in the worst manner. "And you are not mighty against us," meaning you are not dear to us and not honoured, so that we would honour you by refraining from killing you and spare you from stoning. Rather, your people are dear to us, because they are of our religion; they did not choose you over us, nor did they follow you instead of us. If you say: why was it not said, "he leads his people and then brings them to water"? I say: the past tense was used because the past tense indicates a matter that exists and is certain, as if it were said: he will lead them and will certainly bring them to the Fire.

Al-ward (the watering) is the one brought to water (al-mawrud), and al-mawrud is the one who is brought to water by them. He is likened to the forerunner (al-farat) who goes ahead of the animals coming to water, and his followers are likened to the animals coming to water. Then it is said: "evil is the watering-place to which they are brought, the Fire," because watering is only intended to quench thirst and cool the hearts, while the Fire is its opposite.

وَأُتْبِعُوا فِي هذِهِ لَعْنَةً ("and they were followed by a curse in this"), i.e., they are cursed in this world, and they will be cursed in the Hereafter. بِئْسَ الرِّفْدُ الْمَرْفُودُ ("evil is the gift that is given"), i.e., evil is the aid that is aided. That is because the curse in this world is an aid to and reinforcement of the punishment, and they have been aided with a curse in the Hereafter. It is also said: evil is the gift that is given.

with Our signs and a manifest authority. There are two interpretations here. One is that these signs contain a manifest authority for Musa (Moses), proving the truth of his prophethood. The other is that the manifest authority refers to the staff, because it overwhelmed them.

وَما أَمْرُ فِرْعَوْنَ بِرَشِيدٍ ("and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided") is a declaration that his followers are foolish, in that they followed his command, and this is a manifest error that is not hidden from anyone who has even a little sense of reason. This is because he claimed divinity while he was a human like them, and he openly displayed oppression, injustice and evil that come only from a rebellious devil, while he was far removed from divinity both in essence and in actions. Yet they followed him, submitted to his claim and competed in obeying him. Al-amr al-rashid (the rightly guided command) is that in which there is guidance; i.e., there is no guidance in his command, but only clear misguidance and plain, evident error. Sensible people follow only one who guides and directs them, not one who misleads and leads them astray.

In it there is also the point that they witnessed the signs and the manifest authority in the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, and knew that he possessed guidance and truth, yet they turned away from following him to following one whose command had no guidance at all.

يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ ("he will lead his people") means: just as he was a leader for them in misguidance, so he will lead them to the Fire while they follow him.

It is also permissible that by His words, وَما أَمْرُ فِرْعَوْنَ بِرَشِيدٍ, He means: and his command is not good, nor praiseworthy in its outcome. Then His words يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ serve as an explanation and clarification of this; i.e., how could the command of one with such an outcome be rightly guided?

Rushd (guidance) is used for everything that is praised and approved, just as ghayy (error) is used for everything that is blamed and despised.

This is the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 100–101:

That (ذلِكَ) is the subject (mubtada'), "of the reports of the towns (مِنْ أَنْباءِ الْقُرى)" and "We relate it to you (نَقُصُّهُ عَلَيْكَ)" is a predicate following a predicate. That is: that news is part of the reports of the destroyed towns, related to you. "Of them (مِنْها)" — the pronoun refers to the towns (القرى); that is, some of them still stand, and some of them have been effaced from traces, like a crop standing upon its stalk and one that has been harvested.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position (maḥall) of this sentence? I say: it is a resumptive sentence (mustaʼnafa) with no grammatical position.

"And We did not wrong them (وَما ظَلَمْناهُمْ)" — by destroying them. "But they wronged themselves (وَلكِنْ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ)" — by committing that by which they were destroyed. "So their gods availed them not (فَما أَغْنَتْ عَنْهُمْ آلِهَتُهُمُ)" — they were not able to avert the punishment of God from them. "Which they invoked (يَدْعُونَ)" — they worshipped. It is a narration of a past state.

"When (وَلَمَّا)" is in the accusative governed by "availed (أَغْنَتْ)." "The command of your Lord (أَمْرُ رَبِّكَ)" — His punishment and retribution.

"Tatbib (تَتْبِيبٍ)" — ruin and loss. It is said: tabba, when one suffers loss; and tabbabahu, when someone else causes him to suffer loss.

The place of the kāf (ka-) is in the nominative case; its estimate is: "And such is the seizing (akhdh) of your Lord." The accusative is for the one who reads it as "wa-kadhālika akhdhu rabbika," with the verb in its verbal form.

It is also read: "idhā akhadha al-qurā wa-hiya ẓālimatun," where wa-hiya ẓālimatun is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to al-qurā. "Alīmun shadīd" means painful, severe, and hard to bear for the one seized.

This is a warning against the grave consequence of wrongdoing for every people of a wrongdoing town, whether the disbelievers of Makkah or others, and indeed for everyone who wrongs another or himself by a sin he commits. So every person who has sinned should beware of the painful, severe seizing of his Lord, hasten to repentance, and not be deceived by the respite.

That (ذلك, dhalika) refers to the accounts God has related of the nations destroyed for their sins. ﴿Surely in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ means it is a lesson for him, because he looks at what God brought down upon the criminals in this world, and that is only a model of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter. When he sees its magnitude and severity, he takes from it a measure of the magnitude of the promised punishment, so it becomes for him a lesson, an admonition, and a means of grace (lutf) for increasing piety and fear of God, exalted is He. A similar verse is ﴿Surely in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ (79:26).

That (ذلك) refers to the Day of Resurrection, because the punishment of the Hereafter indicates it. ﴿The people﴾ (النَّاسُ, al-nas) is raised as the subject of the passive participle (isim al-maf'ul, the grammatical form expressing the one upon whom an action falls), which is ﴿gathered﴾ (مجموع, majmu'), just as it would be raised by its verb if you said "the people will be gathered for it" (يجمع له الناس).

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask why the expression shifted from the verb to the passive participle..." Ahmad [ibn al-Munayyir] said: For this very secret there came God's words: ﴿Surely We subjected the mountains to glorify with him at evening and at sunrise, and the birds gathered together (mahshurah)﴾ (38:18-19). So He used the verb where it fits, and the passive participle where its use is fitting too...]]

If you ask: For what benefit was the passive participle preferred over its verb? I answer: because the passive participle indicates the permanence of the meaning of gathering for that day, and that it is a day which must be an appointed time for the gathering of people, and that it is characterized by that as a necessary attribute. It is also more emphatic in attributing the gathering to the people, and that they cannot be separated from it. Its parallel is the saying of one who threatens: "You are surely one whose wealth will be plundered, whose people will be fought against," which contains from the firmness and permanence of the attribute what the verb does not. If you wish, compare it with His words ﴿The Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering﴾ (64:9), and you will find the truth of what I told you.

The meaning of ﴿they are gathered for it﴾ is: they are gathered for what it contains of reckoning, reward and punishment. ﴿A witnessed day﴾ means one in which there is witnessing. The expression is extended by treating the time-noun (zarf) as an object (mafʿul bihi), as in the verse:

*"And a day we witnessed, Sulaym and ʿĀmir..."*

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The intended meaning is 'a day witnessed in it', and the expression is extended by treating the time-noun..." Ahmad said: The witnessed thing, which is the object, is left unstated and undefined, and among indefiniteness is that which serves magnification, and this is its place.]]

That is, all creatures witness the standing (al-mawqif); no one is absent from it. The "witnessed" (mashhud) means: that which many have witnessed.

From this is the saying of people: "So-and-so has a witnessed assembly (majlis mashhud)" and "a food that is attended (ta'am mahdur)." The poet said:

*"In a gathering of the foreheads of people, witnessed,*
*From adversaries when the clamor of them is intense,*
*After Ibn Saʿd, and among the lean, the stallions..."*

[[From the adversaries when the uproar with them grows intense... after Ibn Saʿd and among the emaciated (ḍumr) the stallions (qawd).

*And a witnessed assembly, you have sufficed the absent ones by it,*
*In a gathering of the foreheads of the people, witnessed.*
*So you relieved his distress with speech not confused,*
*Among the guardians (ḥufaẓ), and with a heart not fearful.*

Said by Umm Qays al-Ḍabbiyya. "Ḍajja ḍajījan wa ḍajājan" means he cried out. "Ḍajja al-baʿīr min al-ḥaml" means the camel was exhausted by the weight of its load. "Ḍumr" (with the emphatic) is the plural of ḍāmir (lean). A "fras aqwad" is a horse with a long neck; a "rajul aqwad" is one who turns his face toward something and does not turn away. "Al-qird" is its plural. "Mashhad" is in conjunction with "al-khuṣūm" (adversaries). It may also be put in the genitive by "rubba," meaning: an assembly in which you sufficed the absent ones by speaking on their behalf, among a gathering of the chiefs and nobles of the people. "Al-nawāṣī" (the foreheads) is a metaphor for them. "Farrajtahu" means I released his distress and removed his grief with speech clear in its indication, issuing from a tranquil heart, not fearful among the guardians, that is, not the jealousy of adversaries and the guarding of each of them of his opinion, or the anger. It is said: "aḥfaẓahu iḥfāẓan" when he angered him.]]

If you ask: What prevented you from making the day "witnessed" in itself rather than making it "witnessed in it," as God said: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ (2:185)? I answer: the purpose is to describe that day with terror and greatness and to distinguish it from among the days. If you made it witnessed in itself, then all the other days would likewise be witnessed in themselves, all of them. Rather, it is made witnessed in it, so that the distinction is achieved, just as the Day of Friday is distinguished from the days of the week by being witnessed in it and not the others. It was not permissible for it to be witnessed in itself, because all the other days of the week are alike; everyone who attends them witnesses them. Likewise His words:

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ (2:185). "The month" is put in the accusative as a time-noun (ẓarf), not as an object. Likewise the pronoun in ﴿let him fast it﴾ refers to it. The meaning is: whoever of you is present in the month, let him fast in it, that is, whoever of you is resident and present in his homeland during the month of Ramadan, let him fast in it. Had you made it an object, the traveler and the resident would both be witnessing the month; the resident would witness it and the traveler would be absent from it.

Al-Ajal (the appointed term): it is applied both to the whole duration of the deferment and to its endpoint. Thus they say: "The term has ended" (intaha al-ajal), and "The term reached its last part" (balagha al-ajal akhirahu), and they say: "The term has come due" (hall al-ajal). In ﴿So when their term (ajaluhum) comes﴾, it is meant the final portion of the deferment. Counting (al-add) applies only to the duration, not to its limit and end. So the meaning of His words ﴿And We do not delay it except for a term (ajal) numbered﴾ is: "except for the ending of a numbered duration," with the noun being elided (bi-hadhf al-mudaf). It has also been read as ﴿wa-ma yu'akhkhiruhu﴾ with the yā' (ya), i.e. "And He does not delay it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 105:

It has been read as "يَوْمَ يَأْتِ" without the yā' (ya). A similar usage is their saying "لا أدر" (I do not know, without the final "ri"), related by al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh. The omission of the yā' and making do with the kasra (vowel) in its place is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. If you ask: what is the subject (fa'il) of "يأتِ"? I say: it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying ﴿Do they only wait until Allah comes to them?﴾ and ﴿or until your Lord comes﴾ and ﴿and your Lord comes﴾. This is supported by the reading "وما يؤخره" (and He does not delay it) with the yā'. As for His saying ﴿by His permission﴾, it is also possible that the subject is the pronoun of the Day, as in His saying ﴿or the Hour comes upon them﴾. If you ask: by what is the time-adverb (zarf) put in the accusative? I say: either it is accusative by "لا تكلم" (no soul will speak), or by an implied "اذكر" (remember), or by the omitted verb of termination in His saying ﴿except for a term numbered﴾, meaning: the term ends on the Day when it comes. If you ask: when you make the subject the pronoun of the Day, you have made the Day a time for the coming of the Day, and you have delimited a thing by itself. I say: the intended meaning is the coming of what belongs to it and its terrors. "لا تَكَلَّمُ" means "لا تتكلم" (no soul will speak), and this is like His saying ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. If you ask: how can this be reconciled with His saying ﴿the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ and His saying ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be given leave, so they may make excuse﴾? I say: that is a long day with stations and places. In some of them they argue on behalf of themselves; in some of them they refrain from speech and are not given leave; in some of them they are given leave and speak; and in some of them: ﴿a seal is set upon their mouths, and their hands speak to Us and their feet bear witness﴾. The pronoun in "فَمِنْهُمْ" refers to the people of the standing-place, and they were not mentioned because that is known, and because His saying "لا تَكَلَّمُ نَفْسٌ" indicates it. The word "الناس" has already been mentioned in His saying ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾. ﴿Among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾: the wretched is the one for whom the Fire is due because of his wrongdoing, and the blessed is the one for whom Paradise is due because of his goodness.

﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, where they will have sighing and wailing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He wills.﴾

The common reading is with a fatha on the shin (shaqu). It is also related from al-Hasan that it was read with a damma (shuqu), as "suʿidu" was read as "suʿidu" (with a damma on the first letter). Al-zafir is expelling breath, and al-shahiq is returning it. Al-Shammakh said:

*Far is the distance of its tarjee, its first sound is a zafir,*
*and following it is a shahiq, hoarse (mahshraj).*

[[Al-Shammakh describes a wild donkey. Al-mada is the distance and the goal. Al-tatrib is repeating the sound and softening it. Al-zafir is forcefully expelling breath. Al-mahshraj is a passive participle: the sound that one repeats in the throat and chest.]]

As for ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, there are two interpretations. The first is that it refers to the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, which are lasting and created for eternity. The evidence that they have heavens and earth is the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into another earth, and the heavens too﴾ [14:48], and His saying: ﴿And He made us inherit the earth, that we may dwell in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [39:74]. Also, the people of the Hereafter necessarily need something to carry and shade them: either a heaven that God creates, or the Throne shades them, and everything that shades you is a heaven.

The second interpretation is that it is an expression of perpetuity and the negation of cessation, like the Arabic saying: "as long as Taʿar endures," "as long as Thabir stands," "as long as a star shines," and other expressions of eternity.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the exception? I say: it is an exception from eternal abiding in the torment of the Fire and from eternal abiding in the bliss of Paradise. That is because the people of the Fire are not eternal in the torment of the Fire alone, but they are punished with the zamharir (intense cold) and with kinds of torment other than the Fire, and with what is more severe than all of them, which is God's wrath upon them, His rejection of them, and His humiliation of them. Likewise, for the people of Paradise, beyond Paradise there is something greater and more honored in its place for them, which is the good pleasure of God, as He said: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. And approval from God is greater﴾ [9:72]. And they have, beyond the reward of Paradise, what God bestows upon them of favor that cannot be known in its reality except by Him. This is what is meant by the exception. The evidence for it is His saying: ﴿a gift unbroken﴾ [11:108]. The meaning of His saying in contrast: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He wills﴾ is that He does to the people of the Fire what He wills of torment, just as He gives the people of Paradise His gift which has no cessation. So reflect on this, for the Qur'an explains one part of it by another. Do not let the saying of the Mujbira [[His saying "Do not let the saying of the Mujbira deceive you about it" means the People of the Sunna. As for the Mu'tazila, they say that the perpetrator of a major sin is in an intermediate position between the believer and the disbeliever, and his eternal abiding in the Fire is perpetual. The demonstration of its falsehood is in the science of tawhid. (ʿ)]] deceive you, who claim that the exception refers to the people of major sins leaving the Fire through intercession. For the second exception calls out against their lying and records their fabrication.

And what do you think of a people who cast away the Book of God because of what some young men (nawabit) related to them from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs? [[His saying "because of what some young men related to them" — in al-Sihah: "the sons of so-and-so are a nabita of evil," and al-nawabit are youths of young age. (ʿ)]] He said: "There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its doors will clap, with no one in it." [[The hadith was narrated by al-Bazzar, who said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Abu Dawud narrated to us, Shu'ba narrated to us from Abu Bilj, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A time will come upon the Fire when its doors will rattle, with no one in it, meaning from among the monotheists." Thus it is in the text, and its narrators are trustworthy. The interpretation: I do not know from whom it comes, and it is better than the commentator's interpretation. It is supported by what Ibn ʿAdi related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its doors will clap, with no one of the community of Muhammad in it." Also in this chapter, from Abu Umama, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will come upon Hell a day when no one of the children of Adam is in it; its doors will rattle, meaning from among the monotheists." As for the hadith which al-Harith ibn Abi Umama related in his Musnad through the route of al-Hasan from ʿAmr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Hell will be emptied until al-jarjir grows in it," it is disconnected (munqati'). The mursal narrations of al-Hasan are considered weak among them, because he used to take from everyone. If it is preserved, then it is according to the first interpretation, and God knows best.]] This happens after they have remained in it for ages. It has reached me that some of the misguided have been deluded by this hadith, believing that the disbelievers will not abide eternally in the Fire. This and similar views, may God protect us, are from clear abandonment. May God increase us in guidance to the truth, in knowledge of His Book, and in alertness to understand Him. And even if this is authentically from Ibn al-ʿAs, its meaning is that they will be brought out from the heat of the Fire to the cold of the zamharir, and that is the emptiness of Hell and the clapping of its doors.

I say: Ibn ʿAmr had no preoccupation, in his two swords and in his fighting with them against ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that would distract him from transmitting this hadith.

﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, where they will have sighing and wailing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He wills.﴾
