And approval from God is greater﴾ [9:72]. And they have, beyond the reward of Paradise, what God bestows upon them of favor that cannot be known in its reality except by Him. This is what is meant by the exception. The evidence for it is His saying: ﴿a gift unbroken﴾ [11:108]. The meaning of His saying in contrast: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the doer of what He wills﴾ is that He does to the people of the Fire what He wills of torment, just as He gives the people of Paradise His gift which has no cessation. So reflect on this, for the Qur'an explains one part of it by another. Do not let the saying of the Mujbira [[His saying "Do not let the saying of the Mujbira deceive you about it" means the People of the Sunna. As for the Mu'tazila, they say that the perpetrator of a major sin is in an intermediate position between the believer and the disbeliever, and his eternal abiding in the Fire is perpetual. The demonstration of its falsehood is in the science of tawhid. (ʿ)]] deceive you, who claim that the exception refers to the people of major sins leaving the Fire through intercession. For the second exception calls out against their lying and records their fabrication.

And what do you think of a people who cast away the Book of God because of what some young men (nawabit) related to them from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs? [[His saying "because of what some young men related to them" — in al-Sihah: "the sons of so-and-so are a nabita of evil," and al-nawabit are youths of young age. (ʿ)]] He said: "There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its doors will clap, with no one in it." [[The hadith was narrated by al-Bazzar, who said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, Abu Dawud narrated to us, Shu'ba narrated to us from Abu Bilj, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A time will come upon the Fire when its doors will rattle, with no one in it, meaning from among the monotheists." Thus it is in the text, and its narrators are trustworthy. The interpretation: I do not know from whom it comes, and it is better than the commentator's interpretation. It is supported by what Ibn ʿAdi related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its doors will clap, with no one of the community of Muhammad in it." Also in this chapter, from Abu Umama, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will come upon Hell a day when no one of the children of Adam is in it; its doors will rattle, meaning from among the monotheists." As for the hadith which al-Harith ibn Abi Umama related in his Musnad through the route of al-Hasan from ʿAmr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Hell will be emptied until al-jarjir grows in it," it is disconnected (munqati'). The mursal narrations of al-Hasan are considered weak among them, because he used to take from everyone. If it is preserved, then it is according to the first interpretation, and God knows best.]] This happens after they have remained in it for ages. It has reached me that some of the misguided have been deluded by this hadith, believing that the disbelievers will not abide eternally in the Fire. This and similar views, may God protect us, are from clear abandonment. May God increase us in guidance to the truth, in knowledge of His Book, and in alertness to understand Him. And even if this is authentically from Ibn al-ʿAs, its meaning is that they will be brought out from the heat of the Fire to the cold of the zamharir, and that is the emptiness of Hell and the clapping of its doors.

I say: Ibn ʿAmr had no preoccupation, in his two swords and in his fighting with them against ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that would distract him from transmitting this hadith.

Ghayra majdhudhin: not cut off, but extending to no end, like His saying, "For them is a reward that is never cut off" (Qur'an 41:8; 84:25 in other contexts; here the reference is to the verse "a reward unending").

When he had related the accounts of the worshippers of idols, mentioned what Allah had brought upon them of His vengeance and what He had prepared for them of His punishment, he said:

﴿So do not be in doubt about what these worship.﴾ That is: do not doubt, after what has been revealed to you of these accounts, about the evil outcome of their worship and their exposure to it, given what befell the likes of them before them. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a promise of retribution against them, and a warning to them. Then He said: ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped.﴾ He means that their state in polytheism is like the state of their fathers, with no difference between the two conditions. What befell their fathers has reached you, so the like of it will certainly befall them. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), its meaning being the reason for the prohibition against doubt.

The "ma" in "mimma" and in "kama" may be either a verbal-masdar particle (ma masdariyya) or a relative pronoun (ma mawsula), meaning: "from their worship" and "like their worship," or "from what they worship" and "like what they worship of the idols."

﴿And indeed We will pay them their portion﴾: that is, their share of the punishment. [Mahmud said: "That is, their share of the punishment. The word ghayra manqus is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the paid portion (al-nasib al-muwaffa), because it is possible that it be paid while it is deficient and paid while it is complete. Do you not say: 'I paid him half his due' and 'I paid him his due in full'?" Ahmad said: "They (the Mu'tazila) said this, and Allah knows best, for payment (tawfiya) entails that the paid portion is not diminished, whether complete or incomplete. So when you say 'I paid him half his due,' it entails that it was not diminished. What then is the reason for its being placed as a circumstantial state of it? The more appropriate view is to say that tawfiya is used in the sense of giving, just as tawaffi is used in the sense of taking. Whoever says 'I gave so-and-so his due' would be right to emphasize it with the phrase 'not diminished.' And Allah knows best."] Just as We paid their fathers their portions.

If you ask: how is ghayra manqus placed in the accusative as a state of the paid portion? I say: it is possible that it be paid while deficient, and paid while complete. Do you not say: "I paid him a half of his due," "a third of his due," and "his due in full and deficient"?

Ghayra majdhudhin: not cut off, but extending to no end, like His saying, "For them is a reward that is never cut off" (Qur'an 41:8; 84:25 in other contexts; here the reference is to the verse "a reward unending").

The word ghayra manqus is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the paid portion (al-nasib al-muwaffa), because it is possible that it be paid while it is deficient and paid while it is complete. So it was disputed concerning it: a people believed in it and a people disbelieved in it, just as it was disputed concerning the Qur'an. ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, the matter would have been decided between them.﴾ That is, the word of respite (kalimat al-inzar) until the Day of Resurrection, [the matter would have been decided] between the people of Musa or your people. And this is also part of the consolation.

And indeed, the nunation (tanwin, the nunated ending) of *kullan* is a substitute for the genitive complement (*mudaf ilayh*), meaning: "And indeed all of them," that is, all of those who differed concerning it. *La-yuwaffiyannahum* is the answer to an implied oath. The *lam* in *lamma* is the preparatory lam (*lam al-muwattia*) for the oath, and *ma* is redundant (*mazidah*). The meaning is: "And indeed all of them, by God, your Lord will surely repay them their deeds, of good and evil, of faith and denial."

It has also been read as *wa-inna kullan* with the light form, the *inna* operating like the heavy one (*'amal al-mukhaffafah 'amal al-thaqilah*), taking into account its original form, which is the heavy one.

Ubayy read: *wa-inna kulla lamma layuwaffiyannahum*, taking *inna* as negative (*nafiyah*) and *lamma* in the sense of *illa* (except). The recitation of Abdullah explains it: *wa-inna kullun illa layuwaffiyannahum* ("and every one of them, except that your Lord will surely repay them").

Al-Zuhri and Sulayman ibn Arqam read: *wa-inna kullan lamma layuwaffiyannahum*, with tanwin, like the verse ﴿وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا﴾ ("and you devour the inheritance with a devouring, all of it together"). The meaning is: "And indeed all of them gathered together (*mulammin*, meaning *majmu'in*)," as if it were said: "And indeed all of them together," like His words ﴿فَسَجَدَ الْمَلائِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ﴾ ("so the angels prostrated, all of them together").

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 112:

﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded﴾. Steadfast with a steadfastness like the steadfastness you were commanded to have, on the highway of truth, without deviating from it. ﴿And those who turned in repentance with you﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun hidden in "istaqim" (remain steadfast). The conjunction was permitted without emphasizing the pronoun with a separate pronoun, because the intervening element stands in its place. The meaning is: remain steadfast, you, and let those who turned from disbelief and believed with you remain steadfast too. ﴿And do not transgress﴾, that is, do not go beyond the limits of God. ﴿Indeed He is Seeing of what you do﴾, that is, Knowing, so He will recompense you for it; therefore fear Him.

From Ibn Abbas: No verse was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the whole Qur'an that was more difficult or more burdensome for him than this verse. For this reason he said: "Hud and al-Waqi'a and their sisters have made me grey." [[In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Shayban, from Abu Ishaq, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, you have grown grey." He said: "Hud, al-Waqi'a, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and 'Idha al-shams kuwwirat have made me grey." He said: it is a hasan gharib hadith.

Al-Bazzar also narrated it through this route and said: it has been disputed concerning it from Abu Ishaq. Shaybān said so, but Ali ibn Salih narrated from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Hujayya, and Zakariyya narrated from Abu Ishaq, from Masruq, that Abu Bakr said it. Al-Daraqutni expanded on its defects and the variations of its chains at the beginning of the Book of Defects (al-'Ilal). Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Dala'il from the narration of Atiyya ibn Sa'id, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O Messenger of God, greyness has hastened to you." He said: "Hud and its sisters have made me grey: al-Waqi'a, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and 'Idha al-shams kuwwirat." Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Adi also narrated it from the narration of Yazid al-Raqqashi, from Anas, and in it: "al-Waqi'a, al-Qari'a, Sa'al, and 'Idha al-shams kuwwirat."]] It is also related that his Companions said to him: "Greyness has hastened upon you." He said: "Hud has made me grey." It is also reported from one of them: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in a dream and said to him: "It has been related from you that you said: Hud has made me grey." He said: "Yes." I said: "What about it has made you grey? The stories of the prophets and the destruction of nations?" He said: "No, but His saying: ﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded﴾."

From Ja'far al-Sadiq (may God be pleased with him), concerning ﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded﴾, he said: "Be in need of God through the soundness of resolve."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 113:

It has been read as "wa-la tarkanu" (﴿and do not incline﴾), with the kaf vowelled with a fatha or a damma, and the ta with a fatha. It is also reported from Abu 'Amr that the ta was read with a kasra and the kaf with a fatha, according to the dialect of Tamim, who vowel the prefixed letters of the imperfect with a kasra except the yaʼ in every verb of the pattern ʻalima yaʻlamu. A similar reading is that of the one who read ﴿fa-tamassakumu al-nar﴾ (﴿so the Fire will touch you﴾) with a kasra on the ta. Ibn Abi ʻAblah read "wa-la turkanu" in the passive, from arkanahu, meaning he inclined it. The prohibition covers sinking into their desires, attaching oneself to them, keeping their company and sitting with them, visiting them, flattering them, being pleased with their deeds, imitating them, adopting their dress, and casting one's eyes upon their finery. Mentioning them in a manner that honours them is included as well. Consider His words ﴿wa-la tarkanu﴾, for ruku̅n (inclining) is slight leaning.

As for His words ﴿ila alladhina zalamu﴾ (﴿to those who did wrong﴾), meaning: to those in whom wrongdoing was found, and He did not say "to the wrongdoers." It is related that al-Muwaffaq prayed behind an imam who recited this verse, and he fainted. When he came to, he was asked about it, and he said: "This is concerning one who inclines towards those who did wrong; so what of the wrongdoer?" It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: "Allah placed the religion between two prohibitions: ﴿wa-la tatghaw﴾ (﴿do not transgress﴾) and ﴿wa-la tarkanu﴾." When al-Zuhri mixed with the sultans, a brother of his in religion wrote to him: "May Allah protect us and you, Abu Bakr, from trials. You have come to a state in which whoever knows you should pray for Allah to have mercy on you. You have become an old man, and the blessings of Allah have burdened you, since He gave you understanding of His Book and taught you the Sunnah of His Prophet. This is not how Allah took the covenant from the scholars. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Know that the least of what you have committed and the lightest of what you have borne is that you have made the loneliness of the wrongdoer comfortable and made easy the path of error by your nearness to one who has not rendered a right nor abandoned falsehood. When they brought you near, they took you as a pivot upon which the millstone of their falsehood turns, a bridge over which they cross to their calamities, and a ladder by which they climb to their misguidance. Through you they bring doubt upon the scholars and lead the hearts of the ignorant by the reins. How little they have repaired for you in comparison with what they have ruined for you, and how much they have taken from you in comparison with what they have corrupted for you [[The statement "and how much they have taken from you in comparison with what they have corrupted for you" perhaps contains a lacuna, and its intended sense is: "in comparison with what they have given you, and how little they have set right for you in comparison with what they have corrupted..." etc. (ʻ)]] of your religion. What assures you that you will not be among those of whom Allah said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who neglected the prayer and followed their appetites, so they will meet error﴾? You are dealing with one who does not ignore, and you are being watched by one who does not forget. So mend your religion, for sickness has entered it, and prepare your provision, for the long journey has drawn near. Nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven. Peace." Sufyan said: "In Hell there is a valley which is inhabited only by reciters who visit the kings." It is related from al-Awza'i: "There is nothing more hateful to Allah than a scholar who visits a worker (for the rulers)." It is related from Muhammad ibn Maslamah: "A fly on dung is better than a reciter at the door of these people." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays for a wrongdoer to endure has loved that Allah be disobeyed on His earth." [[It was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in the sixty-sixth section of al-Shuʻab, through the narration of Yunus ibn ʻAbd from al-Hasan, as his own statement. Abu Nuʻaym mentioned it in al-Hilyah as a statement of Sufyan al-Thawri.]] It was asked of Sufyan about a wrongdoer who was about to perish in a desert: should he be given a sip of water? He said: "No." It was said to him: "He will die?" He said: "Leave him to die."

﴿Wa-ma lakum min dun Allahi min awliya'﴾ (﴿and you have no protectors other than Allah﴾) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from His words ﴿fa-tamassakumu﴾, meaning: the Fire will touch you while you are in this state. Its meaning: you have no helpers other than Allah who can prevent you from His punishment; none other than Him can prevent you from it. ﴿Thumma la tunsarun﴾ (﴿then you will not be helped﴾): then He Himself will not help you, because in His wisdom it has become necessary to punish you and not to spare you. If you ask: what is the meaning of "thumma" (then)? I say: its meaning is remoteness, because help from Allah is remote given that they deserve punishment and His wisdom requires it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 114:

"Both ends of the day" (ṭarafayi al-nahār): the morning (ghadwa) and the evening (ʿashiyya). "And at intervals of the night" (zulafan min al-layl): these are the hours of the night close to its end, from azlafahu, meaning he brought it near, and izdalafa ilayhi, meaning he drew near to it. The prayer of the morning (ghadwa) is the Fajr prayer. The prayer of the evening (ʿashiyya) is the Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr prayers, because what comes after the decline of the sun (zawāl) is ʿashiyy. The prayer at the intervals (zulaf) is the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers.

The word ṭarafayi (both ends) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), because both are attached to a time-word. Like your saying: "I stayed with him the whole day (jamīʿ al-nahār), and I came to him at midday (niṣf al-nahār), at its beginning (awwalahu) and its end (ākhirahu)." You put all of these in the accusative by giving the genitive-construct (muḍāf) the ruling of the word it is attached to (muḍāf ilayhi). Similar to this is the phrase "wa-aṭrāfa al-nahār" (and the ends of the day).

It has been recited as "wa-zulfan" with two dammas, and as "wa-zulfan" with a sukūn on the lām, and as "zulfā" on the pattern of "qurbā." Thus zulaf is the plural of zulfa, like ẓulam being the plural of ẓulma. Zulf with sukūn is like busra and bus, and zulf with two dammas is like busr in busr. Zulfā has the same meaning as zulfa, just as qurbā has the same meaning as qurba. It means what comes near the end of the day from the night.

It has also been said that "wa-zulfan min al-layl" means "and nearness of the night" (wa-qurban min al-layl). According to this interpretation, it should be conjoined to the prayer, meaning: "Establish the prayer at both ends of the day, and establish zulfan of the night," in the sense of: "Establish a prayer by which you draw near to God, Mighty and Majestic, in part of the night."

"Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds" (inna al-ḥasanāti yudhhibna al-sayyiʾāt). There are two possible meanings. The first is that the minor sins are expiated by acts of obedience. It is in a ḥadīth: "The prayer from one prayer to the next is an expiation for what is between them, as long as the major sins are avoided." [[Al-Ḥākim narrated it from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayra, raised to the Prophet: "The obligatory prayer to the obligatory prayer is an expiation for what is between them, as long as the major sins are avoided."]] The second is that good deeds remove bad deeds by being a means of gentleness (luṭf) in abandoning them, like God's saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing﴾.

It has been said: this verse was revealed concerning Abū al-Yasar ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyya al-Anṣārī. He used to sell dates, and a woman came to him and he was attracted to her. He said to her: "In the house there are dates better than these." So he took her to his house, embraced her and kissed her. She said to him: "Fear God!" So he left her and regretted it. He came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and told him what he had done. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wait for the command of my Lord." When he prayed the ʿAṣr prayer, the verse was revealed. He said: "Yes, go, for it is an expiation for what you did."

It is also narrated that he came to Abū Bakr and told him, and he said: "Conceal your sin and repent to God." Then he came to ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, and he said to him the same. Then he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed. ʿUmar said: "Is this for him alone, or for people in general?" He said: "Rather, it is for people in general."

It is also narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Perform ablution well, and pray two rakʿas," then: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾.

[[In the original it was "Abū al-Yasar ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyya," and this is an error. It is in fact Abū al-Yasar Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr. So it is also in the books on the names of the Companions. The author (al-Zamakhshari) followed al-Thaʿlabī, for he said likewise: "It was revealed concerning ʿAmr ibn Ghaziyya al-Anṣārī." The ḥadīth is in al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Ṭabarī, from the narration of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mawhab, from Mūsā ibn Ṭalḥa ibn Abī al-Yasar ibn ʿAmr, who said: "A woman came to me to buy dates. I said to her: 'In the house there are dates better than these.' So she entered the house with me. I leaned toward her and kissed her. She said: 'Fear God!' So I came to Abū Bakr and mentioned that to him. He said: 'Conceal your sin and repent.' So I came to ʿUmar and he said the same. So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and he lowered his head for a long time until it was revealed to him: ﴿Establish the prayer ...﴾ the verse. Ibn Abī al-Yasar said: I went to him and he recited it to me. His companions said: 'O Messenger of God, is this for him alone, or for people in general?' He said: 'Rather, it is for people in general.'"

In a narration of Aḥmad: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "O Messenger of God, is it for him alone, or for all people?" And for al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Ḥākim and al-Bayhaqī, from the narration of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla, from Muʿādh: he was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a man came and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you say about a man who had unlawful intercourse with a woman, and did not leave anything a man may do with his wife except that he did it with her, except that he did not have intercourse with her?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Perform ablution well, then pray." So God, Exalted, revealed the verse. Muʿādh said: "Is it for him alone, or for the Muslims in general?" He said: "Rather, it is for the Muslims in general." The root of this ḥadīth is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Bukhārī and Muslim) from Ibn Masʿūd: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I was with a woman at the far end of Medina, and I touched her without having intercourse. Here I am, so judge me as you wish." ʿUmar said to him: "God would have concealed you if you had concealed yourself." The Prophet (ﷺ) did not answer him at all. So the man left, and the Prophet (ﷺ) sent after him a man, and he called him and recited to him: ﴿Establish the prayer at both ends of the day ...﴾ the verse. A man of the people said: "O Messenger of God, is it for him alone, or for people in general?" He said: "Rather, it is for people in general."]]

"That" (dhālika) refers to His saying: ﴿So be steadfast﴾, and what follows it. "A reminder for those who remember" (dhikrā li-l-dhākirīn): an admonition for those who take heed.

Then he returned to exhorting patience after having mentioned what concludes the exhortation. This return is for the special excellence and distinction of patience, and to draw attention to its place and station, as if he said: "And hold to what is more important than what you were reminded of and more deserving of enjoining, namely patience in carrying out what you were commanded and in refraining from what you were forbidden, for none of it is complete except through it." Then ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ came with what encompasses steadfastness (istiqamah), establishing the prayers, refraining from transgression, not inclining toward the wrongdoers, patience, and other good deeds.

Fa-law-lā kāna min al-qurūn (fa-hallā kāna): "Why then was there not, among the generations..." It has been related from al-Khalil that every *lawlā* in the Qur'an means *hallā* (why not), except the one in al-Saffat. But even if this report is not sound, it applies to other than al-Saffat: *lawlā an tadārakahu niʿmatun min rabbihi la-nubidha bil-ʿarāʾ* ("Had it not been that a blessing from his Lord had reached him, he would have been cast out onto the barren land"), *wa-lawlā rijālun muʾminūn* ("And had there not been believing men..."), and *wa-lawlā an thabbatnāka la-qad kidta tarkanu ilayhim* ("And had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them").

Ulū baqiyyah (ulū baqiyyatin): "possessors of a remnant," or "possessors of virtue and goodness." They called excellence and generosity *baqiyyah* because a man keeps back the best and finest of what he brings out, so it became a proverb for goodness and excellence. One says: "So-and-so is of the remnant of the people," meaning, of their best.

It is explained by the verse of the Hamasa (anthology):

If you commit offences, then your remnant comes to me... 
[[O rider urging on his mount, ask the Banu Asad what this cry is about.
And say to them: hurry to make excuses and seek a word that will clear you, for I am Death.
If you commit offences, and then your remnant comes to me, there is no failing on my part because of your offence.

It is by Rushayd ibn Kathir al-Ta'i. Zajja (with light or heavy shaddah) and azjā mean: drove it onward. By "the cry" he meant the shout or the story that reached him about him, and he described himself as Death as hyperbole. "Baqiyyat al-qawm" means their best, and it can also be a verbal noun meaning "remaining," like *taqiyyah* meaning *tuqwa*. The meaning on the first reading: if you offend, and then your most distinguished men come to me to make excuses for you, then there is no failure, and no harm to me because of the offence of others. On the second reading: then there comes to me from you the one who cares for his own self, who says: "Do not destroy us for what the foolish among us did," and so on.

It is also possible that the meaning is: if you gather together either to fight or to make excuses, then your punishment will not escape me, rather it is unavoidable. The retention of the yā' in *ya'tīnī* is for lengthening (ishbāʿ), but the latter is not suitable given his words "hurry to make excuses."]] From this comes their saying: "In corners there are hidden things, and among men there are remnants." It is also possible that *baqiyyah* means *baqwā* (remaining), like *taqiyyah* for *tuqwā*, meaning: "Why was there not among them one possessing remaining and preserving himself from the wrath and punishment of God?"

It is also read *ulū baqiyyah* in the pattern of *laqiyyah*, from *baqāhu yabqīhi*, meaning to watch over and await him, and from it: "We waited for the Messenger of God (ﷺ)..." [[Abu Dawud related it from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "We waited for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for the 'Isha' prayer, and he delayed until one thought he would not come out... the hadith."]] *Baqiyyah* in that case is the single instance of the verbal noun. The meaning: "If there had been among them people of watchfulness and fear of God's vengeance, as if they were waiting for His striking them, out of their apprehension..."

*Illā qalīlan*: an exceptive construction that is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: "But a few of those whom We saved from the generations forbade corruption, while the rest abandoned the forbidding." The *min* in *mimman anjaynā* should be explanatory (bayān) rather than partitive, because salvation was only for those who forbade, alone, as evidenced by God's words: "We saved those who forbade evil, and seized those who did wrong." If you ask: Is there a way to take this exception as connected? I say: If you make it connected according to the apparent sense of the speech, the meaning would be corrupt, for it would be an urging of the people of remnant to forbid corruption, except for the few of the saved among them, as you say: "Why did your people not read the Qur'an, except the righteous among them?" You intend to exclude the righteous from those urged to read the Qur'an. But if in their urging to forbid corruption you understand the meaning of its negation regarding them, as if it were said: "There were not among the generations people of remnant except a few," then the exception is connected and the meaning is sound, and its accusative case is on the basis of the original exception, although the more eloquent form is the nominative as a substitute (badal).

*Wa-ittaba'a alladhīna ẓalamū mā ufrifū fīhi*: by "those who did wrong" he means those who abandoned forbidding evil deeds, that is, they did not concern themselves with what is a great pillar of the religion, namely commanding right and forbidding wrong. They set their resolve upon desires and followed what they had been made comfortable in, of love of leadership and wealth, and seeking the pleasant means of life. They rejected what lay beyond that and cast it behind their backs. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of al-Ju'fi, read *wa-ittaba'a alladhīna ẓalamū* (with the verb in the active), meaning: they followed the consequence of what they had been made to enjoy. The meaning in the familiar reading may also be that they followed the consequence of their luxury. This is a strong meaning because of the preceding mention of deliverance, as if it were said: "except a few of those whom We saved from them, and the rest perished." If you ask: On what is the phrase *wa-ittaba'a alladhīna ẓalamū* conjoined? I say: If its meaning is "they followed the desires," it is conjoined to an implied element, because the meaning is: "except a few of those whom We saved from them, who forbade corruption, while those who did wrong followed their desires," so it is conjoined to *nahaw* (they forbade). If its meaning is "they followed the consequence of luxury," then the *wāw* is circumstantial (ḥāl), as if it were said: "We saved the few while those who did wrong had followed their punishment." If you ask: What of His words *wa-kānū mujrimīn*? I say: It is conjoined to *ufrifū*, meaning they followed luxury and were criminals, because one who follows desires is overwhelmed by sins. Or the meaning of criminality is their neglect of gratitude. Or it is conjoined to *ittaba'ū*, meaning they followed their desires and were criminals by that. It is also possible that it is a parenthetical statement and a judgment upon them, that they are a criminal people.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 117:

"Kāna" (كان) here means "it is correct and proper" (ṣaḥḥa wa-istaqāma). The "lām" is for emphasizing the negation. "Wa-bi-ẓulmin" (وبِظُلْمٍ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject. The meaning is:

It is impossible, according to wisdom, that God should destroy the towns with injustice while their people are reformers (ṣāliḥūn, مُصْلِحُونَ), in order to declare His essence free from injustice, and to make clear that destroying the reformers is an injustice. It has also been said: the injustice (ẓulm) is polytheism (shirk), and the meaning is that God does not destroy the towns on account of the polytheism of their people while they are reformers who deal justly among themselves and do not add to their polytheism any other corruption.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 118–119:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. That is, He would have compelled them to be people of one community, i.e., one religion, which is the religion of Islam, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this, your community, is one community﴾. This statement implies the negation of compulsion, and that He did not compel them to agree upon the religion of truth. Rather, He granted them choice (ikhtiyar), which is the basis of moral obligation (taklif). So some of them chose truth and some of them chose falsehood, and they differed. Therefore He said: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾, that is, except those whom God guided and showed kindness, so they agreed upon the religion of truth without differing concerning it. ﴿And for that He created them﴾: this is an indication of what the first statement indicated and implied, meaning: for that, i.e., for the granting of power and choice from which the difference arose, He created them, so that He might reward the one who chooses truth for his good choice, and punish the one who chooses falsehood for his bad choice. ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾, which is His saying to the angels: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together﴾, because of His knowledge of the great number of those who would choose falsehood.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verses 120–122:

The tanwin in "wa-kullan" (وَكُلًّا) is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted, as if it were said: "and each [of the narratives]." The phrase "Wa-kulla naba'in naqussu 'alayka" ("and every news We relate to you") is an explanation of "kullan." "Wa-min anba'i al-rusuli" ("and from the news of the Messengers") is an explanation of "kull." "Ma nuthabbitu bihi fu'adaka" ("that with which We strengthen your heart") is a substitute (badal) for "kulla."

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "Each [kind of] relating (iqtisas) that We relate to you," in the sense of: "Each type of relating that We relate to you," meaning: in its various methods. In that case, "ma nuthabbitu bihi" is the object of "naqussu."

The meaning of strengthening his heart (tathbit fu'adihi) is an increase in his certainty and that which brings tranquility to his heart, because the accumulation of proofs is more firmly establishing for the heart and more lasting for knowledge. "Wa-ja'aka fi hadhihi al-haqqu" means: in this (surah), i.e., the truth.

Or, [it means]: in these narrated news, among which is what is true. "Wa-mawi'zatun wa-dhikra lil-mu'minin" ("and an admonition and a reminder for the believers"). "Wa-qul lilladhina la yu'minun" ("And say to those who do not believe"), from the people of Makkah and others: "i'malu 'ala halikum wa-jihatikum allati antum 'alayha" ("Act according to your state and your direction in which you are"), "inna 'amilun" ("indeed we are acting"), "wa-antaziru bina al-dawa'ira" ("and wait, [you], for the turns of fortune concerning us"), "inna muntazirun" ("indeed we are waiting") that there descend upon you the like of what Allah has related of the punishments that descended upon your counterparts.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 11, verse 123:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the entire matter is returned.﴾ Nothing hidden within them that occurs in them is concealed from Him, so your deeds are not concealed from Him. And to Him the entire matter is returned, so their affair and yours must necessarily return to Him, and He will take vengeance for you against them. ﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him.﴾ For He is sufficient for you and your guardian. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do.﴾ It is also read: ﴿what you do﴾, with the ta' (second person).

That is, you and they, by way of giving precedence to the addressee (taghlib al-mukhatab).

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Whoever recites Surah Hud will be given the reward of ten good deeds, equal to the number of those who believed in Noah and those who denied him, and Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Lut, Ibrahim and Musa; and he will be among the blessed on the Day of Resurrection, if Allah the Exalted wills. [[Its chain of narration was mentioned earlier in Al 'Imran and will come at the end of the book.]]
